author: corrie-ten-boom
fields.title: Portraits of Courage – Corrie ten Boom
fields.subtitle: A Hiding Place in Haarlem, a Sister in Ravensbrück, and the Long Work of Forgiveness
fields.description: A Christian biography of Corrie ten Boom (1892–1983), the Haarlem watchmaker whose family hid Jews from the Nazis, whose father and sister died after their arrest, and who spent forty years preaching God’s forgiveness. It follows her from the Beje through Scheveningen, Vught, and Ravensbrück to Munich and sixty countries — comparing her earliest 1945 account with The Hiding Place and the independent record. Told in its own words, with gratitude but not hagiography; all Scripture from the public-domain ASV (1901).

qa.question: What is this biography of Corrie ten Boom about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of Corrie ten Boom (1892–1983), the Dutch watchmaker whose family hid Jewish refugees in a secret room in their Haarlem home. It follows her whole life — the family watch shop, the underground work, the raid of 28 February 1944, the prison at Scheveningen, the camps at Vught and Ravensbrück where her sister Betsie died, and the forty years of travel and preaching about forgiveness that followed.

qa.question: Who was Corrie ten Boom?
qa.answer: Corrie ten Boom was a Dutch Christian and the first woman qualified as a watchmaker in the Netherlands. During the German occupation she and her family sheltered Jews and resistance workers in their home, the Beje, in Haarlem. After their arrest her father died in prison and her sister Betsie at Ravensbrück; Corrie survived and became an internationally known speaker. Yad Vashem recognised her as Righteous Among the Nations in 1967.

qa.question: How does this book differ from The Hiding Place?
qa.answer: The Hiding Place (1971) is Corrie’s own story, written with John and Elizabeth Sherrill. This biography tells her life in its own words and compares it with her earliest account, the 1945 book A Prisoner and Yet, and with independent records. It notes which famous scenes appear already in 1945 — the vitamin bottle, the hiding-place drills — and which appear only later, such as the fleas in the barracks and the ‘clerical error’ release.

qa.question: Did everyone in the hiding place survive?
qa.answer: No. Six people stood in the hiding place during the raid and were not found. But one of them, Mary van Itallie, was arrested again within days and murdered at Auschwitz in May 1944, according to the Jewish memorial register of the Netherlands. The cantor Meijer Mossel, called Eusie, survived the war. The book tells their story honestly rather than stopping at the raid.

qa.question: Was Corrie’s release from Ravensbrück really a clerical error?
qa.answer: Corrie believed so, having been told this years later. But no document confirms it, her 1945 account shows the sisters expecting a fixed prison term, and Ravensbrück’s gas chamber began operating about a month after her release, not a week. The book concludes that she was discharged for reasons never fully explained, and that the danger she escaped was real.

qa.question: What did Corrie ten Boom teach about forgiveness?
qa.answer: That forgiveness is an act of the will which God makes possible when we cannot. She wrote to the man believed to have betrayed her family in June 1945, forgiving him, and later told of shaking the hand of a former Ravensbrück guard in Munich only when God’s love flowed through her. She was honest that she had to learn forgiveness again and again.

qa.question: How is Scripture used in the book?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a passage from the American Standard Version (1901) that carries its theme — beginning with ‘Thou art my hiding-place and my shield’ — and further passages are woven through the story, from Psalm 91, read by her brother on the night of the arrest, to Romans 5:5. Every quotation was checked against the ASV text.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning. The preface and introduction explain the sources; Part One tells of the family and fifty years of quiet faithfulness; Part Two the occupation and the hiding place; Part Three the prisons and Ravensbrück; Part Four the long work of forgiveness. Appendix B offers a chapter-by-chapter study guide for groups.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“Thou art my hiding-place and my shield: I hope in thy word.”

— Psalm 119:114, ASV

The first volume of this series told the story of Watchman Nee, a Chinese church leader who spent his last twenty years in a Communist prison. The second told the story of John Hyde, an American missionary in the Punjab whose courage was mostly hidden, spent on his knees in prayer rooms and village huts. This third volume tells the story of a woman whose courage was hidden in a different way, behind a false wall in a bedroom at the top of a narrow house in Haarlem.

Corrie ten Boom is probably the best-known person in this series. Millions of people have read her story or watched the film made from it. Her name is familiar far beyond the churches: on lists of people who rescued Jews during the Holocaust, in the Dutch national canon of history, and in the tree planted in her honour at Yad Vashem in Jerusalem. That familiarity is a gift, and it is also a difficulty. A life that everyone knows tends to become a set of famous scenes: the secret room, the fleas in the barracks, the bottle of vitamins that did not run dry, and the handshake with a former guard in Munich. Each scene is told so often that it can come loose from the life around it.

This book tries to put the scenes back into the life. It follows Corrie from her birth in Amsterdam in 1892 to her death in California on her ninety-first birthday in 1983. It gives full room to the nearly fifty years of quiet, unremarkable life she lived in a Dutch watch shop before the war. It also follows her through the ten months of prison and concentration camp that made her famous, and through the more than thirty years of travelling and preaching that came after.

Why Courage?

It may seem obvious why Corrie ten Boom belongs in a series called Portraits of Courage. She and her family broke the laws of an occupying power to hide people whom that power meant to murder. They were caught, and her father and sister died because of it. That is courage of the most visible kind.

But the longer one looks at her life, the more it seems that her most important courage came before and after the dramatic part. Before the war there was the courage of ordinary faithfulness: the small, repeated choices of a family who, by their own tradition, had prayed for the Jewish people every week for generations, and who kept their door open to anyone in need. After the war there was the courage it took to forgive. That was not a single heroic act. It was a costly habit she had to learn again and again, beginning with a letter to the man who had betrayed her family. It is harder to film than a raid, and it is the heart of what she spent the rest of her life trying to say.

How This Book Is Written

Corrie ten Boom told her own story many times, in many books. The best known, The Hiding Place, was written with John and Elizabeth Sherrill and published in 1971. Earlier and less known is the account she wrote in the months after her release, published in Dutch in June 1945 and in English two years later as A Prisoner and Yet. All of her books remain in copyright, and they should be read in her own words. This book does not reproduce them. It tells her life in its own words, quoting her only in a few brief phrases. It draws on the independent historical record wherever possible: Dutch war-graves records, the Jewish memorial registers, the Yad Vashem file, the archives of the prison where she was held, and the museum that now occupies her home.

Like the Hyde volume before it, this book tries to be honest about its sources. Some things about Corrie’s life are documented in records made at the time. Some rest on her own testimony, which is precious evidence but is still one person’s memory. Some are later additions, the natural growth of a story told thousands of times over forty years. This book will try to say which is which. It does not do so to cast doubt on her. The core of her story is confirmed at every point by independent records. It does so because she herself would have wanted the glory to go to God and the truth to be told straight.

Scripture in This Book

As in the earlier volumes, all Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, which is in the public domain. Each chapter opens with a passage that carries its theme, and further passages are woven through the narrative.

The verse at the head of this preface is from Psalm 119: “Thou art my hiding-place and my shield: I hope in thy word.” The title by which the world knows Corrie’s story, The Hiding Place, has a double meaning, and she intended both. There was the secret room in her bedroom, where six people stood in the dark for two and a half days while the house was searched and then guarded. And there was the hiding place she found when that room could no longer protect her, when she was alone in a cell or standing on a frozen parade ground at Ravensbrück. She found it in God himself, and in his word. The first hiding place was built by an architect whose real name we still do not know. The second was not built by human hands at all. This book is the story of how an ordinary woman came to know both.

fields.title: Introduction: The Story She Told, and the Story the Records Tell
fields.body_html:
“Ye are my witnesses, saith Jehovah, and my servant whom I have chosen; that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he”

— Isaiah 43:10, ASV

A Witness Who Told Her Story Many Times

Most of the people in this series left few words of their own. John Hyde wrote almost nothing, and his story survives mainly in two little books written by friends after his death. Corrie ten Boom is the opposite case. She told her own story for nearly forty years, to audiences in more than sixty countries, and she put it into print again and again. Few Christian lives of the twentieth century are so fully narrated by the person who lived them.

That is a great advantage for a biographer, and it is also a challenge. A story told thousands of times does not stay exactly the same. Details are sharpened, and scenes are arranged for the listener. A lesson that took years to learn is compressed into a single moment. Things understood only later are read back into the moment itself. None of this is dishonesty. It is simply what happens to memory, especially the memory of a preacher whose purpose is to help others meet God. But it means that the careful reader should know which version of the story is being told, and when it was first told.

The Earliest Account

Corrie’s first book was written within months of her return from Ravensbrück. It was published in Amsterdam in June 1945, a month after the liberation of the Netherlands, as Gevangene en toch …, “A prisoner, and yet …”. An English translation appeared in London in 1947 under the title A Prisoner and Yet, with a foreword by Norman Grubb of the Worldwide Evangelization Crusade. It is a short, vivid, sometimes unpolished book. It moves quickly from the busy underground household in Haarlem to the raid, the prison at Scheveningen, the camp at Vught, and the long nightmare of Ravensbrück. Much of it reads like notes made while the events were still raw. It even reproduces her discharge certificate from the camp, with her prisoner number on it.

This early book is precious because of its closeness to the events. It was written before Corrie became a famous speaker, before she had told the story to thousands of audiences, and before any ghostwriter shaped it. Where it agrees with her later accounts, and it does on nearly every essential point, it confirms them. Where it differs, it gives us a glimpse of the story before long retelling had smoothed it.

The Famous Account

Twenty-six years later, in 1971, Corrie published the book that made her world-famous. The Hiding Place was written with the American writers John and Elizabeth Sherrill, who interviewed her at length and shaped her memories into a gripping narrative. It became a bestseller, and in 1975 it was made into a film by World Wide Pictures, the film company of the Billy Graham organisation. For most readers since, The Hiding Place simply is Corrie ten Boom’s story.

The Hiding Place is far fuller than the 1945 book. It tells of her childhood, her father’s shop, the family’s life before the war, her lost love, and the long work of forgiveness after the war. It is beautifully written. But it was written a quarter of a century after the events, by professional writers, for an audience of American Christians, and some of its best-loved scenes do not appear in the earlier account. Comparing the two books is one of the ways this biography tries to be faithful to her.

What the Comparison Shows

The comparison is reassuring on the essentials. The 1945 book already has the busy household of refugees, with Eusie the cantor singing too loudly at the piano. It has the hidden room behind the false wall, the drills with a stopwatch, and the cream puffs afterwards. It has the raid on 28 February 1944, the slaps in the face, and the plaque on the fireplace that read “Jesus is Victor.” It has her father’s words about giving his life for “God’s ancient people.” It has the months of solitary confinement, the ants in her cell, and the vitamin bottle at Ravensbrück that went on giving drops long after it should have run dry. It has Betsie’s death, and the sisters’ plans for a home for released prisoners.

Some things appear only later. The 1945 book says nothing of the fleas that kept the guards out of the barracks where the sisters held their Bible readings. It mentions lice, and says that others avoided the barracks because of them. It does not tell of the man who came to the shop on the morning of the raid asking for money to free his wife, the man later named as the informer. It does not call Corrie’s release a clerical error. Rather, it shows the two sisters expecting their prison term to end at a fixed date. Betsie’s famous words, that there is no pit so deep that God’s love is not deeper still, are recorded in the later book. In the 1945 book a related thought appears in Corrie’s own mouth. Some of these later details may well be true memories that Corrie simply did not include in 1945. Others may have grown in the telling. This book will usually tell them, but will say where they first appear.

The Independent Record

Alongside Corrie’s own accounts there is a substantial independent record, and it confirms the core of her story at every point.

The Dutch war-graves foundation records her father’s death in The Hague on 9 March 1944, nine days after his arrest. It also records the death of her nephew Kik in Bergen-Belsen in 1945. Betsie’s death at Ravensbrück on 16 December 1944 is recorded on the memorial plaque at the family home. The Jewish memorial registers of the Netherlands record the fate of Mary van Itallie, one of the Jewish guests in the house. The prison memorial at Scheveningen records Corrie’s imprisonment there. Yad Vashem, Israel’s Holocaust memorial, recognised Corrie as Righteous Among the Nations in 1967, and her father and Betsie in 2007. Hans Poley, one of the young men who hid in the house, published his own memoir with his wartime diaries in 1993. The museum that now occupies the house, opened in 1988, preserves the family’s papers and its own careful chronology.

This record also corrects some popular claims, and this book will follow it. Corrie was born in Amsterdam, not Haarlem. Not all of the six people who stood in the hiding place during the raid survived the war. One of them, Mary van Itallie, was arrested again within days and died at Auschwitz. The often-repeated figure of eight hundred people saved, Jews and others, is the museum’s estimate for the whole network of which the family was part, not a count of those hidden in the house. And the frequent claim that the informer was executed after the war is not supported by the records of Dutch postwar executions.

How This Book Proceeds

Part One, A House of Clocks, tells of the family and the fifty years of ordinary faithfulness that prepared them for the war. Part Two, The Hiding Place, follows the occupation, the underground work, and the raid. Part Three, Ravensbrück, follows Corrie and Betsie through prison and camp until Betsie’s death and Corrie’s release. Part Four, A Tramp for the Lord, follows the years of travel and witness that followed, and her last silent years.

The verse at the head of this chapter is God’s word to Israel through Isaiah: “Ye are my witnesses.” Corrie understood her life after Ravensbrück as exactly that, a witness. She was not a witness to her own courage, which she always played down, but to the faithfulness of God in the darkest place human beings have made. A witness should be heard in her own words. For that, readers should go to her books. What this book can offer is a careful, honest account of the life behind the testimony, told with gratitude, and with the hope that it points, as she always did, beyond herself.

fields.title: The Beje
fields.body_html:
“Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: They shall prosper that love thee.”

— Psalm 122:6, ASV

A Narrow House on a Busy Street

In the old centre of Haarlem, a few steps from the great market square and the towering Grote Kerk of St. Bavo, runs a short shopping street called the Barteljorisstraat. At number 19 stands a narrow house, only one room wide at the front, that seems to have been squeezed between its neighbours. Behind the shopfront it climbs and turns in ways that no architect would plan: steep stairs, half-landings, rooms at odd levels, and passages that are said to join what were once two separate buildings. Parts of it are said to date from around 1600. The family who lived there for more than a century called it the Beje, pronounced roughly “bay-yay,” from the initials of the street name, B and J.

The house is famous now. It is a museum, visited by tens of thousands of people a year, and it is listed among the places that tell the story of the Netherlands in the official national canon of Dutch history. Visitors climb the narrow stairs to a small bedroom at the top of the house. They peer through a low opening under a cupboard shelf into a space about the width of a man’s shoulders, where six people once stood hidden while soldiers searched the rooms around them. But for most of its history the Beje was nothing more than what it looked like from the street: a watchmaker’s shop with a family living above it.

A Shop Founded in 1837

The shop was opened in 1837 by a watchmaker named Willem ten Boom, Corrie’s grandfather. According to the family’s records, now kept by the museum, he began with a capital of one hundred guilders. It was a modest start for a modest business. For more than a hundred years, three generations of ten Booms repaired and sold clocks and watches from that small front room. They wound the town’s clocks, regulated its pocket watches, and knew its people by the timepieces they carried.

A watchmaker’s trade suited that family. It is patient, precise work, done with small tools and a steady hand, and it depends entirely on trust. A customer leaves a precious object and must believe it will be returned whole and honestly repaired. The ten Booms kept that trust for a century. It would matter more than they could imagine when the time came for their neighbours to trust them with something far more precious than a watch.

A Prayer Begun in 1844

Family tradition, preserved by the museum, holds that in 1844 Willem ten Boom began a practice that would shape his descendants more than any other. He was moved by a sermon from a Haarlem minister, the Rev. Witteveen, on the verse at the head of this chapter: “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: They shall prosper that love thee” (Psalm 122:6, ASV). From then on, the story goes, he gathered a small group once a week to pray for the Jewish people and for the peace of Jerusalem. It was an unusual prayer for a Dutch Protestant shopkeeper in the 1840s. It was nearly a century before the modern state of Israel would exist, and Jerusalem was a small Ottoman town.

No document from 1844 survives to confirm the date, and the claim that the prayer continued for exactly a hundred years is a round, commemorative figure. But it fits well with what we know of the religious world Willem lived in. In the first half of the nineteenth century the Netherlands was stirred by a movement called the Réveil, the “awakening.” It was an evangelical revival among Dutch Protestants that stressed personal faith, Bible reading, prayer, and practical charity. One of its leading figures was the poet Isaac da Costa, a converted Jew from Amsterdam, and the Réveil was marked by a warm interest in the Jewish people and their place in God’s purposes. A pious watchmaker in Haarlem, moved by such preaching to pray each week for Jerusalem, would have been entirely at home in that world.

Whatever its exact beginnings, the prayer became part of the family’s identity. Corrie’s father grew up with it, and so did Corrie. When the Nazis occupied the Netherlands a century later and began to hunt down Dutch Jews, the ten Booms did not have to be persuaded that the Jews were their concern. Psalm 122 is a song of pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the festivals. “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go unto the house of Jehovah” (Psalm 122:1, ASV). Its prayer for the city’s peace is also a prayer for its people. “For my brethren and companions’ sakes, I will now say, Peace be within thee” (Psalm 122:8, ASV). To pray for Jerusalem, in the psalmist’s sense, is to love the people of God and to long for their good.

The psalm adds a promise: “They shall prosper that love thee.” It is worth pausing over that promise in the light of what happened to the ten Booms. By most earthly measures, they did not prosper for loving the Jewish people. Casper died in prison. Betsie died in a concentration camp. A grandson, Kik, died in Bergen-Belsen. Casper’s son Willem died of an illness he caught in prison. The home itself was taken from them. If “prosper” means safety and comfort, the promise seems to have failed.

But Scripture’s idea of prosperity is larger than that. Jesus said, “Blessed are they that have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:10, ASV). The ten Booms’ love for the Jewish people cost them almost everything this world could take. It also gave them the thing Corrie spent the rest of her life describing: an experience of God’s faithfulness in the darkest place, so real that she could not stop talking about it. In the end their name was honoured in Jerusalem itself: Corrie, and later her father and Betsie, were recognised among the Righteous Among the Nations, and a tree was planted there for Corrie. That is a strange kind of prosperity, but it is not nothing.

The Return to Haarlem

Willem ten Boom’s son Casper, Corrie’s father, learned the watchmaking trade from him. As a young married man, Casper set up his own shop in Amsterdam, in a neighbourhood with many Jewish families. The move seems to have taken place in 1892, soon after Corrie’s birth. From then on, the Beje was Corrie’s home until the day of the raid, when she was nearly fifty-two.

The house they moved into was already crowded. Casper’s wife, Cor, had three sisters, and over the years all three came to live in the Beje with them. With five children, three aunts, the shop, the workroom, and a constant stream of visitors, the narrow house was always full. Corrie later remembered it as a place where there was always room for one more at the table. That habit of making room was learned long before anyone needed hiding.

A small detail from Corrie’s earliest account gives the flavour of the house. On the day of the raid in February 1944, as her aged father was led out of the Beje for the last time, he paused in the hall beside the old Frisian clock that hung there and suggested that Corrie pull up its weights. It is a touching picture. An old watchmaker, arrested for hiding Jews, thinks as he leaves of the clock that needs winding. But it is also a picture of the whole ten Boom household. For a hundred years they had done the small faithful thing that was needed next. They wound the clocks and kept the shop, they prayed each week for Jerusalem, and they set another place at the table. They did not know that all of this was preparation. It was simply how they lived.

We often think of courage as something that appears suddenly in a crisis. The story of the Beje suggests otherwise. The courage the ten Booms showed in 1943 and 1944 had been growing for a century. It was rooted in a grandfather’s weekly prayer, in a trade built on trust, and in a crowded household that had learned to make room. When the crisis came, they did what they had always done, but at a much higher cost.

What are the small, repeated faithfulnesses in our own homes? What do we pray for every week, and whom do we make room for? We may never face a test like the ten Booms’ test. But if one comes, it will probably find us doing whatever we have practised for years.

fields.title: A Father Among the Watches
fields.body_html:
“and I will bless them that bless thee, and him that curseth thee will I curse: and in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed.”

— Genesis 12:3, ASV

Casper

Casper ten Boom was born in Haarlem on 18 May 1859, the son of the watchmaker Willem ten Boom. He grew up in the Beje, learned his father’s trade at the bench in the back workroom, and, apart from his early married years in Amsterdam, spent almost his entire life within a few streets of the house where he was born. By the standards of the world, his life was small. He was a skilled craftsman and a respected shopkeeper. At one time, according to the Dutch war-graves foundation, he served as chairman of Haarlem’s chamber of commerce. He never grew rich, travelled little, and wrote nothing that has survived beyond family letters. Yet his daughter would spend forty years telling the world about him, and those who met him seem never to have forgotten him.

In October 1884 Casper married Cornelia Luitingh, a schoolteacher, whom the family called Cor. The young couple began their married life in Amsterdam, where Casper opened a watch shop of his own at Korte Prinsengracht 28. Their neighbourhood was home to many Jewish families, and family tradition remembers that Casper had close Jewish friends there. It says he sometimes joined them for their Sabbath and festival meals. We do not have the details, and later retellings may have warmed the picture. But it helps to explain what came later. To Casper ten Boom, Jews were not a distant religious category. They were neighbours, friends, and fellow lovers of the Scriptures.

“God’s Ancient People”

Casper’s view of the Jewish people was shaped by his reading of the Bible, and it was not complicated. God had chosen Israel, made promises to Abraham, and given them the law and the prophets. Through Israel the Messiah had come. God had not withdrawn his love.

The verse at the head of this chapter is God’s first promise to Abraham. “I will bless them that bless thee, and him that curseth thee will I curse: and in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 12:3, ASV). Paul, writing to the church in Rome many centuries later, insisted that God’s calling of Israel still stood. He called them the people “whose is the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and of whom is Christ as concerning the flesh” (Romans 9:4-5, ASV). “Did God cast off his people?” he asked. “God forbid” (Romans 11:1, ASV). “For the gifts and the calling of God are not repented of” (Romans 11:29, ASV).

Casper had a phrase for the Jews that his daughter remembered all her life: they were “God’s ancient people.” It is not a phrase invented by later writers. It appears in Corrie’s first account, written in 1945. Friends had warned the old man that if he went on sheltering so many Jews he would end up in prison, and that in his frail state he would never survive it. He answered that if that happened, he would count it an honour to give his life for God’s ancient people. It did happen, and he did.

A Star He Meant to Wear

An incident from 1942, recorded by the Dutch war-graves foundation, shows how seriously Casper took his convictions. That spring the German authorities ordered every Jew in the Netherlands to wear a yellow star on their clothing, marked with the word “Jood.” Casper, then in his eighties, intended to go and collect a star for himself and wear it in solidarity with his Jewish neighbours. He was talked out of it, presumably by family members who could see where such a gesture would lead. But the intention tells us who he was. He did not think of the Jews’ suffering as their problem. He thought of it as his own.

A Father in the House

Most of what we know about Casper as a father comes from Corrie’s own memories, written down decades later, and they should be read as a daughter’s portrait. They are affectionate, and they may be idealised. But they are consistent, and they match what outsiders said of him.

In her telling he was gentle, humorous, and deeply prayerful. The household gathered every day to read the Bible and pray, and Casper read aloud from the great family Bible at meals. He was absent-minded about money and generous to a fault. He was known to spend more time talking with a customer about God than fixing the customer’s watch. He treated the children who came to the shop and the beggars who came to the back door with the same courtesy he showed the town’s wealthy families.

Corrie’s 1945 account gives two glimpses of him at eighty-four that ring true. In the busy months of 1943, when the house was full of Jewish refugees and young resistance workers, Mary, the eldest of the Jewish guests, taught an Italian class in the evenings. Casper came to the class with his notebook, because learning languages was one of his hobbies. And on the day of the raid, when a German officer, seeing a Bible in the room, demanded to know what it said about the government, the old man quoted Peter: “Fear God; honour the Queen.” When the officer protested that the Bible said nothing of the kind, Casper politely corrected himself. It said “the king,” he explained, but in the Netherlands that meant the Queen. The verse is 1 Peter 2:17, which in the ASV reads, “Fear God. Honor the king.” It was a quiet act of defiance, delivered with courtesy, in front of the men who were about to take him to prison.

The people of Haarlem seem to have loved him. Corrie’s first account says the town called him “Haarlem’s Grand Old Man,” and that as the prisoners were driven away from the police station, neighbours stood silently in the street with tears in their eyes.

“The Best Is Yet to Come”

Corrie recorded one of her father’s favourite sayings in her 1945 book: “The best is yet to come.” He said it often, she recalled. On the bus from Haarlem to the prison, when he was weak and confused and leaning heavily on her arm, she and Betsie spoke with him about heaven, and he agreed that whatever happened, heaven awaited them. After his death, a niece wrote to Betsie in prison telling her not to grieve. Grandfather’s motto had been “the best is yet to come,” and now the best had come for him.

It was not a naive optimism. Casper did not expect the best from the German occupation, and he was not surprised when it came for his family. His hope looked beyond this life. It was the hope Paul expressed from prison: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21, ASV). A man who truly believes that the best is yet to come is free to take risks that other people cannot take. He has already settled what matters most.

A Son Who Studied Antisemitism

Casper’s love for the Jewish people passed to all his children, but it took a scholarly form in his only surviving son. Willem ten Boom, born in 1886, became a minister of the Dutch Reformed Church. In 1928 he earned a doctorate at the University of Leipzig in Germany with a dissertation on the origins of modern racial antisemitism. He was studying, years before Hitler came to power, the very ideas that would soon be used to justify the murder of Europe’s Jews.

From 1925 Willem also served as a minister of the Dutch Society for Israel, a Protestant organisation whose work combined care for Jewish people with Christian mission among them. That combination can be uncomfortable for modern readers, and it should be named honestly. The ten Booms’ love for the Jewish people was a Christian love. They longed for Jews to know Jesus as their Messiah, and they said so. But in the years that mattered most, that love did not wait for anyone to agree with them. The ten Booms sheltered Jews as Jews, because they were people in mortal danger and God’s ancient people. They asked for nothing in return. Willem’s care home at Hilversum sheltered Jews during the war, and his son Kik worked in the resistance and died in a concentration camp.

For Reflection

Casper ten Boom was an old watchmaker with no power and no platform. What he had was a settled conviction, drawn from Scripture, that the Jewish people were beloved by God. He lived that conviction in the ordinary courtesies of a lifetime, long before it became dangerous.

Most of us hold convictions that have never been tested. We could ask which of them we would be willing to wear on our sleeve, as Casper wanted to wear the yellow star. And we could ask whether we are practising those convictions now, in small ways, so that they will be ready if the test ever comes.

fields.title: The Youngest Daughter
fields.body_html:
“God setteth the solitary in families: He bringeth out the prisoners into prosperity”

— Psalm 68:6, ASV

Born on Good Friday

Cornelia Arnolda Johanna ten Boom was born in Amsterdam on 15 April 1892. That year the date fell on Good Friday. Family tradition, recorded by the museum that now occupies the Beje, adds that she arrived a month early and was so small and frail that no one expected her to live long. She lived to be ninety-one, and died on her birthday.

Many popular accounts say she was born in Haarlem. She was not. The Dutch women’s biographical lexicon, the museum’s own chronology, and the Holocaust memorial encyclopedias all give Amsterdam, where her father then had his shop. It is a small correction, but the kind of detail that shows how a famous story settles into a simpler shape over time. Corrie was brought to Haarlem as a baby, grew up there, and belonged to it so completely that the town has claimed her ever since.

She was the youngest of five children. The eldest, Elisabeth, always called Betsie, was born in August 1885 and was nearly seven years older. Then came Willem in 1886. A second son, Hendrik Jan, born in 1888, died in infancy. Arnolda, known as Nollie, was born in 1890. The family called the new baby Corrie, and the name stuck for the rest of her life, even on the covers of her books.

A House Full of Women

The Beje of Corrie’s childhood was crowded, loud, and full of strong personalities. Besides her parents and her brother and sisters, three of her mother’s sisters lived there for long periods. Tante Anna had lived with the family since the Amsterdam days and stayed until 1925. Tante Jans and Tante Bep joined the household in Haarlem.

Corrie’s later portraits of these aunts, written for The Hiding Place and In My Father’s House, are among the most vivid parts of her books. In her telling, one aunt ran committees and wrote religious tracts with great energy and not much tact. Another had spent her working life as a governess in wealthy homes and quietly resented her dependence on others. Another served everyone without complaint. These are a novelist’s sketches, affectionate and a little comic, and they should be read as a grown woman’s memories of childhood. But they tell us something important. Corrie grew up in a household where love had to make room for difficult people. That was a training ground for patience long before she had any idea she would need it.

Her Mother

Corrie’s mother, Cor, had been a teacher before her marriage. In Corrie’s memory she was warm, sociable, and generous, the kind of woman who made up baskets for poor neighbours and remembered every birthday. But she was not strong. A series of strokes marked her last years, and by Corrie’s account she was left able to say only a few words. She died on 17 October 1921, aged sixty-three.

Corrie was twenty-nine. She had watched her mother’s world shrink to a single room and a few sounds, and she later wrote that her mother’s love had gone on expressing itself through the little she could still do. The memory stayed with her. Nearly sixty years later, after her own strokes, Corrie lay in a room in California for five years, almost unable to speak. One of the women who cared for her then wrote a whole book about those silent years, and about the love that still came through them. The daughter had learned from the mother how to be helpless well.

School, and a Bible School

Corrie’s schooling was ordinary for a Dutch girl of her class. She went to primary school and then to a domestic-science school, the kind of practical training that was expected to prepare a young woman for running a household. Around 1910 she also spent some years at a Bible school in Haarlem. There is no sign that she was an outstanding student, or that anyone thought her destined for anything unusual. She loved music, played the piano, and was lively and talkative. She was much less orderly than her older sister Betsie, who was quiet, graceful, and meticulous.

Karel

Corrie never married, and the reason she gave, many years later, was a disappointment in love. In The Hiding Place she tells of a young man named Karel, a friend of her brother Willem from his student days. She came to hope that he would marry her. As she remembered it, he visited, walked with her, and seemed to return her feelings. But his family expected him to make a better match, a young woman with money and position, and in the end he did. He came to the Beje to introduce his fiancée.

This story rests entirely on Corrie’s own account. No independent record identifies Karel, and it would be wrong to guess at his surname. But the way she told it is worth attention. She remembered climbing to her room afterwards in misery. Her father came up to her and, as she tells it, spoke not of forgetting the young man but of what to do with love that has nowhere to go: rather than stifle it, she could give it to God and let him redirect it. Corrie told that story to many audiences. She believed it had shaped her whole life. The love she might have given to a husband and children went instead to the girls in her clubs, to the disabled people she taught, to the foster children who later came to the Beje, to the Jews she hid, and in the end to the whole world.

The Solitary in Families

The verse at the head of this chapter speaks of God as the one who “setteth the solitary in families” (Psalm 68:6, ASV). Corrie and Betsie both remained single all their lives. In the Dutch society of their day, an unmarried woman in her forties was often pitied, and sometimes quietly overlooked. The two sisters lived with their father and kept his house and shop. In the eyes of the town, they were simply the watchmaker’s daughters.

But they were never alone. The Beje was a family in the fullest sense. It was a household of aunts, nieces and nephews, and later foster children. In the war it held Jewish refugees and young resistance workers for whom the old watchmaker became “Grandfather.” God set the solitary in families, and he also made the solitary into a family for others. Isaiah, speaking to a desolate city, promised, “For more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife, saith Jehovah” (Isaiah 54:1, ASV). By the end of her life, people all over the world thought of Corrie ten Boom as a kind of spiritual grandmother. That was not the life she had hoped for as a young woman climbing the stairs after Karel’s visit. It was a larger one.

The second half of the psalm verse is also worth noticing, in the light of what was to come: “He bringeth out the prisoners into prosperity.” That line would take on a meaning in Corrie’s life that no one in the Beje of 1921 could have imagined.

For Reflection

Corrie’s early life contained two great losses: a mother who declined through a series of strokes, and a hoped-for marriage that did not happen. Neither made headlines, and both shaped her deeply.

Her father’s counsel is worth remembering. When love is disappointed, the easier course is to harden the heart so that it stops hurting. The harder course is to offer that love to God and let him direct it where he will. For Corrie, it led to a life of loving far more people than one household could ever have held.

fields.title: The First Woman Watchmaker
fields.body_html:
“He that is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much: and he that is unrighteous in a very little is unrighteous also in much.”

— Luke 16:10, ASV

Behind the Counter

For most of the twentieth century’s first two decades, Corrie ten Boom’s life was the life of a daughter at home. She helped to run the crowded household, nursed her failing mother, and took her part in the family’s church and charitable work. The shop downstairs was her father’s world, and for a time it was Betsie’s, who kept the books and served the customers. Corrie, by her own later account, was the one who cooked and cleaned.

Around 1920 that changed. In The Hiding Place Corrie tells how a spell of illness kept Betsie from the shop. Corrie took her place behind the counter, and Betsie took over the household, and each found that the swap suited her. Betsie had a gift for making a home beautiful on very little. Corrie discovered that she loved the shop, and above all the workbench. Whatever exactly happened, by the early 1920s the two sisters had settled into the roles they would keep for twenty years. Betsie ran the house, and Corrie worked with her father in the shop.

Learning the Trade

Casper taught Corrie watchmaking at his own bench, as his father had taught him. But she did not rely on his teaching alone. According to Dutch sources, she went abroad to train, serving an apprenticeship with a watchmaker in Switzerland, the heart of the European watch industry. Basel is the town most often named. It was an unusual step for a Dutch woman of her time and class. Watchmaking was a skilled trade, and like almost every skilled trade it was dominated by men.

At some point in the early 1920s Corrie gained her professional qualification. The museum’s chronology and the Dutch women’s biographical lexicon both say that in 1924 she became the first woman in the Netherlands to qualify as a watchmaker. Other sources give 1921 or 1922, and no one seems to have seen the certificate itself. The exact year hardly matters. What matters is that in her early thirties, with no expectation of marriage and no great prospects, Corrie ten Boom became a master of a demanding craft. According to the museum, she was the first woman in her country to do so.

It is a detail that her later fame has tended to overshadow, and it deserves to be remembered. Before she was a rescuer, a prisoner, or a preacher, Corrie ten Boom was a skilled professional woman. She broke a small barrier in her own trade, quietly, without making anything of it.

Small Mechanisms

The work itself is worth imagining. A watch of the 1920s was a marvel of tiny parts: springs as fine as hair, jewels on which the wheels turned, and screws that had to be handled with tweezers under a magnifying glass. Repairing one required patience, steadiness, good eyesight, and an almost stubborn attention to detail. One grain of dust in the wrong place could stop the whole mechanism. One impatient movement could ruin a part that would take days to replace.

Corrie spent the best part of twenty years at such work, day after day, in the back room of the Beje. It is not fanciful to think that it shaped her. Watchmakers learn to work slowly and carefully, and to trust the small things. They learn that a mechanism will only keep good time if every part does its work, however small or hidden. They learn to keep going on a repair when nothing seems to be happening, because the result will only show at the end.

Those were exactly the habits the underground would need. The work of hiding people was also a matter of small mechanisms. There were ration cards to be collected and delivered, and false identity papers to be obtained. Safe addresses had to be found and checked. Messages had to be carried, and drills practised with a stopwatch in hand until the guests could vanish in seventy seconds. The courage of the ten Booms was not only a matter of bold decisions. It was a matter of patient, careful, repetitive work, done right every time, because one careless slip could cost lives.

“Faithful in a Very Little”

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from one of Jesus’ hardest parables, about a dishonest steward. But the saying Jesus draws from it is plain enough: “He that is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10, ASV). Faithfulness is not a quality that appears suddenly when great things are at stake. It is built, or neglected, in small things.

Scripture repeatedly honours ordinary work done well. Paul told the Colossians, “Whatsoever ye do, work heartily, as unto the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23, ASV). The book of Proverbs asks, “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings” (Proverbs 22:29, ASV). Corrie ten Boom, the careful watchmaker of Haarlem, did in fact end up standing before royalty. In 1962 Queen Juliana made her a knight of the Order of Orange-Nassau, and she visited the former Queen Wilhelmina more than once. But the diligence came first, in the back room, on repairs no one would ever praise.

A Shop as a Cover

There was one more way in which the shop prepared the family for what was coming. A watchmaker’s shop has a constant flow of visitors. People come and go all day long, bringing in watches, collecting them, asking questions, and paying bills. Nobody notices one more customer at the door.

When the house became a hub of the underground in 1943, that constant traffic became a cover. Corrie’s 1945 account describes the stream of young resistance workers pouring into the Beje from early morning, and her room upstairs as a kind of clearing house for supply and demand. It would have been far harder to hide such traffic at a private house. The shop that Grandfather Willem had opened with a hundred guilders in 1837 turned out to be exactly the right front for the work of 1943.

A Hundred Years

In The Hiding Place, Corrie opens her story with a celebration. In January 1937 the shop turned one hundred years old, and friends, customers, and neighbours crowded the little house to congratulate her father. As she tells it, her brother Willem arrived with news of Jewish refugees fleeing Germany, and the shadow of what was coming fell across the party. It is a writer’s device, the happy occasion with a hint of darkness at its edge, and it may have been shaped for effect. But the date is right, and the shadow was real. In Germany the Nuremberg Laws had already stripped Jews of their citizenship, and thousands were trying to get out. In the Netherlands, a watch shop celebrated its centenary, and the family who kept it went on praying for Jerusalem as they had for nearly a hundred years.

For Reflection

Corrie ten Boom’s twenty years at the watchmaker’s bench are the least dramatic part of her life, and perhaps among the most important. There she learned patience, precision, faithfulness in small things, and the stubborn habit of doing a job properly whether or not anyone noticed.

Most of our lives are made of such work. It is easy to think of it as a waiting room, the dull time before God calls us to something significant. Corrie’s life suggests another view. The faithfulness God asks of us in small things is not a waiting room. It is the workshop where he makes us into people who can be trusted with much.

fields.title: Clubs, Children, and the Least of These
fields.body_html:
“And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye did it unto one of these my brethren, even these least, ye did it unto me.”

— Matthew 25:40, ASV

A Single Woman with Time to Give

By the time she was thirty, Corrie ten Boom’s life seemed settled. She would work in her father’s shop, keep house with Betsie, and grow old in the Beje. That was the ordinary fate of an unmarried daughter in a Dutch shopkeeping family, and she does not seem to have resented it. But she did not let it make her small. In the twenty years between her mother’s death and the German invasion, Corrie poured herself into a series of quiet works among young people, disabled people, and children in need. None of them made the newspapers. All of them, looking back, were preparation.

The Triangle Girls

The best known of these works was a network of clubs for girls and young women. The Dutch sources call them the Driehoekmeisjes, the “Triangle girls.” The name came from the clubs’ emblem, a triangle whose three sides stood for body, soul, and spirit. The idea was that Christian faith is not only a matter of Sunday religion. It concerns the whole person: physical health and recreation, the mind and the feelings, and the life of the spirit before God. The clubs offered sport, music, crafts, outings, and summer camps, alongside Bible study and prayer.

Corrie was a natural leader of such things. She was energetic, funny, and unselfconscious, and she enjoyed young people. She organised camps, led singing, and gave talks. The clubs grew over the years. Under the German occupation independent youth work was suppressed, but Corrie’s 1945 book records that at least one of her clubs, a group of older girls, went on meeting faithfully while she was in prison.

It is easy to overlook this work, but it gave Corrie two things she would later need badly. It gave her experience of organising: of recruiting helpers, managing money, planning logistics, and keeping many threads in her hands at once. And it gave her a wide network of young people who trusted her. When the underground needed couriers, hosts, and helpers in 1942 and 1943, some of the young people who came to the Beje were the kind of young people Corrie had spent twenty years leading.

Teaching Those Others Overlooked

From around 1921, the Dutch sources record, Corrie also began teaching the Christian faith to people with intellectual disabilities. In the Netherlands of the 1920s such people were largely hidden away, in institutions or back rooms, and few churches thought them capable of understanding the gospel. Corrie thought otherwise. She held special classes for them and prepared them for church membership. She seems to have treated this as some of the most important work she did.

In her later books Corrie told stories of these classes: the patient repetition, the simple words, the joy of a student who grasped that God loved him. Those stories come from her own memory and should be read as such. But the outline is confirmed by the Dutch sources, and it tells us something about her. Long before the war, Corrie had chosen to spend her time on people the world considered unimportant.

There is a darker thread here that she could not have foreseen. Within a few years the German regime that would occupy her country began murdering disabled people in its own hospitals, under a programme it called euthanasia. The people Corrie had been teaching were exactly the kind of people that ideology considered unworthy of life, and when a Gestapo officer later questioned her, he would tell her that her work among them was a waste of time. She would answer him from twenty years of experience.

Children in the Beje

The ten Booms also opened their home to foster children. The museum records that in the 1920s and 1930s several children lived with the family for periods of time. By Corrie’s account, some were the children of missionaries serving overseas. The narrow house, already full of aunts and relatives, took them in. Corrie, Betsie, and their father became a kind of second family to them.

We know few details, and the family seems not to have thought the arrangement remarkable. It was simply another expression of the habit of making room. But it meant that by 1942, when the first Jewish refugees knocked at the Beje’s door, the household had long experience of absorbing strangers into its daily life. It knew how to stretch the food, give up a bed, make someone at home, and keep the peace in crowded rooms. The underground home that Corrie later described, with its classes, concerts, and jokes, did not come from nowhere. It was built on twenty years of practice.

“One of These My Brethren”

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Jesus’ parable of the sheep and the goats. The Son of man, sitting on his throne, separates the nations and welcomes those who fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, took in the stranger, clothed the naked, and visited the sick and the prisoner. They are surprised: when did they do all this for him? And the King answers, “Inasmuch as ye did it unto one of these my brethren, even these least, ye did it unto me” (Matthew 25:40, ASV).

What is striking about the parable is that the righteous did not know they were serving Christ. They were not performing religious duties. They were simply responding to the needs in front of them, and they did it so naturally that they had forgotten it. That is a good description of the ten Boom household in the years between the wars. They were not planning heroism. They were teaching disabled young people, running girls’ clubs, and taking in foster children, because that is what their faith meant to them.

The parable has another edge that the ten Booms would soon feel. Among “the least” Jesus names the stranger and the prisoner. Within a few years Corrie and her family would take in strangers who were being hunted, and they would themselves become prisoners. They would learn from the inside what it means to depend on the kindness of others, and to find Christ present in a prison cell.

A Quiet Life, Nearly Fifty Years Long

When the Germans invaded the Netherlands in May 1940, Corrie ten Boom was forty-eight years old. For nearly half a century she had lived an ordinary life, and by the standards of the world an insignificant one. She had spent it among clocks, children, aunts, and the small works of a devout household. She was a single woman in a provincial town, known to her neighbours as the watchmaker’s daughter.

That is worth pausing over, because the popular story of Corrie ten Boom begins in 1942 or 1943, as though her life only started when she became a rescuer. It did not. The woman who organised an underground network, stood up to interrogators, and survived Ravensbrück had been formed over five decades of small faithfulness. She was nearly fifty when the events began for which the world remembers her. Anyone who suspects that their real life has not yet started might take some comfort from that.

For Reflection

Corrie’s work between the wars had no audience and no glamour. It was clubs for girls, classes for disabled people, and foster children in a crowded house. None of it seemed to be leading anywhere. All of it turned out to be preparing her.

Who are “the least” in our own communities, the people the world overlooks? Serving them rarely feels significant. But Jesus says that what we do for them, we do for him. And sometimes, as the ten Booms found, the habits of love we form in quiet years are exactly what God will use when the storm comes.
fields.body_text: “And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye did it unto one of these my brethren, even these least, ye did it unto me.” — Matthew 25:40, ASV A Single Woman with Time to Give By the time she was thirty, Corrie ten Boom’s life seemed settled. She would work in her father’s shop, keep house with Betsie, and grow old in the Beje. That was the ordinary fate of an unmarried daughter in a Dutch shopkeeping family, and she does not seem to have resented it. But she did not let it make her small. In the twenty years between her mother’s death and the German invasion, Corrie poured herself into a series of quiet works among young people, disabled people, and children in need. None of them made the newspapers. All of them, looking back, were preparation. The Triangle Girls The best known of these works was a network of clubs for girls and young women. The Dutch sources call them the Driehoekmeisjes, the “Triangle girls.” The name came from the clubs’ emblem, a triangle whose three sides stood for body, soul, and spirit. The idea was that Christian faith is not only a matter of Sunday religion. It concerns the whole person: physical health and recreation, the mind and the feelings, and the life of the spirit before God. The clubs offered sport, music, crafts, outings, and summer camps, alongside Bible study and prayer. Corrie was a natural leader of such things. She was energetic, funny, and unselfconscious, and she enjoyed young people. She organised camps, led singing, and gave talks. The clubs grew over the years. Under the German occupation independent youth work was suppressed, but Corrie’s 1945 book records that at least one of her clubs, a group of older girls, went on meeting faithfully while she was in prison. It is easy to overlook this work, but it gave Corrie two things she would later need badly. It gave her experience of organising: of recruiting helpers, managing money, planning logistics, and keeping many threads in her hands at once. And it gave her a wide network of young people who trusted her. When the underground needed couriers, hosts, and helpers in 1942 and 1943, some of the young people who came to the Beje were the kind of young people Corrie had spent twenty years leading. In the Netherlands of the 1920s such people were largely hidden away, in institutions or back rooms, and few churches thought them capable of understanding the gospel. Corrie thought otherwise. She held special classes for them and prepared them for church membership. She seems to have treated this as some of the most important work she did. In her later books Corrie told stories of these classes: the patient repetition, the simple words, the joy of a student who grasped that God loved him. Those stories come from her own memory and should be read as such. But the outline is confirmed by the Dutch sources, and it tells us something about her. Long before the war, Corrie had chosen to spend her time on people the world considered unimportant. There is a darker thread here that she could not have foreseen. Within a few years the German regime that would occupy her country began murdering disabled people in its own hospitals, under a programme it called euthanasia. The people Corrie had been teaching were exactly the kind of people that ideology considered unworthy of life, and when a Gestapo officer later questioned her, he would tell her that her work among them was a waste of time. The narrow house, already full of aunts and relatives, took them in. Corrie, Betsie, and their father became a kind of second family to them. We know few details, and the family seems not to have thought the arrangement remarkable. It was simply another expression of the habit of making room. But it meant that by 1942, when the first Jewish refugees knocked at the Beje’s door, the household had long experience of absorbing strangers into its daily life. It knew how to stretch the food, give up a bed, make someone at home, and keep the peace in crowded rooms. The underground home that Corrie later described, with its classes, concerts, and jokes, did not come from nowhere. It was built on twenty years of practice. “One of These My Brethren” The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Jesus’ parable of the sheep and the goats. The Son of man, sitting on his throne, separates the nations and welcomes those who fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, took in the stranger, clothed the naked, and visited the sick and the prisoner. They are surprised: when did they do all this for him? And the King answers, “Inasmuch as ye did it unto one of these my brethren, even these least, ye did it unto me” (Matthew 25:40, ASV). What is striking about the parable is that the righteous did not know they were serving Christ. They were not performing religious duties. They were simply responding to the needs in front of them, and they did it so naturally that they had forgotten it. That is a good description of the ten Boom household in the years between the wars. They were not planning heroism. They were teaching disabled young people, running girls’ clubs, and taking in foster children, because that is what their faith meant to them. The parable has another edge that the ten Booms would soon feel. Among “the least” Jesus names the stranger and the prisoner. Within a few years Corrie and her family would take in strangers who were being hunted, and they would themselves become prisoners. They would learn from the inside what it means to depend on the kindness of others, and to find Christ present in a prison cell. A Quiet Life, Nearly Fifty Years Long When the Germans invaded the Netherlands in May 1940, Corrie ten Boom was forty-eight years old. For nearly half a century she had lived an ordinary life, and by the standards of the world an insignificant one. She had spent it among clocks, children, aunts, and the small works of a devout household. She was a single woman in a provincial town, known to her neighbours as the watchmaker’s daughter. That is worth pausing over, because the popular story of Corrie ten Boom begins in 1942 or 1943, as though her life only started when she became a rescuer. It did not. The woman who organised an underground network, stood up to interrogators, and survived Ravensbrück had been formed over five decades of small faithfulness. She was nearly fifty when the events began for which the world remembers her. Anyone who suspects that their real life has not yet started might take some comfort from that. For Reflection Corrie’s work between the wars had no audience and no glamour. It was clubs for girls, classes for disabled people, and foster children in a crowded house. None of it seemed to be leading anywhere. All of it turned out to be preparing her. Who are “the least” in our own communities, the people the world overlooks? Serving them rarely feels significant. But Jesus says that what we do for them, we do for him. And sometimes, as the ten Booms found, the habits of love we form in quiet years are exactly what God will use when the storm comes.

fields.title: May 1940
fields.body_html:
“For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then will relief and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place, but thou and thy father’s house will perish: and who knoweth whether thou art not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”

— Esther 4:14, ASV

Five Days in May

In the early hours of 10 May 1940, German forces crossed the Dutch border. The Netherlands had stayed neutral in the First World War and had hoped to stay neutral again. Its army was small and poorly equipped, and it fought bravely for five days. On 14 May German bombers destroyed the centre of Rotterdam, killing hundreds of civilians. The German command threatened to do the same to Utrecht and other cities, and on 15 May the Dutch army surrendered. Queen Wilhelmina and her government had already escaped to London, where they would lead a government in exile for the rest of the war. The country was placed under a German civilian administration headed by the Austrian Nazi Arthur Seyss-Inquart.

In Haarlem, as everywhere else, ordinary life went on at first more or less as before. Shops opened, trains ran, and the watchmaker’s shop in the Barteljorisstraat took in watches for repair. German soldiers appeared in the streets. For many Dutch people the first months of occupation were more humiliating than frightening. The occupiers were, at first, careful to appear correct and reasonable. They hoped to win the Dutch, whom Nazi ideology regarded as fellow “Germanic” people, to their side.

The Tightening

For the Jews of the Netherlands, the occupation was something else entirely. About 140,000 Jews lived in the country in 1940, most of them in Amsterdam. Over the next two years the German authorities isolated them step by step, with a thoroughness that the Dutch civil service, trained to obey lawful orders, often helped to carry out.

Jewish civil servants were dismissed in 1940. In early 1941 every Jew had to register, and from early 1942 Jews’ identity cards were stamped with a large J. In February 1941, after German police rounded up hundreds of young Jewish men in Amsterdam, workers in the city went on strike in protest. It was one of the very few mass public protests against the persecution of Jews anywhere in occupied Europe, and it was crushed within two days. Jews were then barred from parks, cinemas, cafés, libraries, public transport, and non-Jewish schools. Their businesses were taken over. In May 1942 they were ordered to wear a yellow six-pointed star on their clothing, with the word “Jood” in the centre.

In July 1942 the deportations began. Jews received notices to report for “labour service in Germany.” They were gathered at a transit camp at Westerbork in the north-east of the country, and from there nearly every Tuesday a train left for the east, most often to Auschwitz or Sobibor. By the end of the war more than 100,000 Dutch Jews had been murdered, about three in every four. It was one of the highest proportions of any country in Western Europe.

What Could an Old Watchmaker Do?

The ten Booms watched all this from their shop window. Casper was eighty in 1939. Betsie was in her mid-fifties, and not strong. Corrie was nearly fifty. They had no weapons, no political influence, no connections in government, and no money to speak of. What could they possibly do?

We have already seen one answer. When the yellow star was introduced in May 1942, Casper wanted to wear one himself. That would have been a public act of solidarity, and a foolish one, since it would have achieved nothing except his own arrest. His family talked him out of it. But the instinct behind it was right. The persecution of the Jews was not something happening to other people. It was happening to God’s ancient people, the people the family had prayed for every week for a century. It was happening to neighbours and customers whose watches hung on the hooks in the shop.

Corrie’s own turning point, as she described it in 1945, came in the home of a Jewish doctor. She was visiting him one evening, discussing something ordinary, when his small child called down the stairs to remind him that he had not come up to tuck her in. The doctor excused himself at once, and Corrie heard him upstairs romping with the children before they slept. As she sat waiting, she realised what could happen to this family at any moment. The Gestapo might come for these children in the night, and the father might be taken away. Then and there, she wrote, a resolution took shape in her heart: she would help the Jews wherever she could.

It is a small scene, and it has the ring of truth because it is so small. There was no vision or voice, and no dramatic call. A child asked to be tucked into bed, and a woman in a Dutch sitting room decided that she could not stand by.

“For Such a Time as This”

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the book of Esther, which tells of an earlier attempt to destroy the Jewish people. A powerful official in the Persian empire, Haman, had persuaded the king to issue a decree for the killing of all the Jews in his realm. The queen, Esther, was herself secretly Jewish. Her cousin Mordecai urged her to go to the king and plead for her people. To go into the king’s presence uninvited meant risking death. Esther hesitated, and Mordecai sent her a message: “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then will relief and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place, but thou and thy father’s house will perish: and who knoweth whether thou art not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14, ASV).

Two things in Mordecai’s words are worth holding together. The first is confidence in God’s purposes. If Esther refuses, deliverance will come “from another place.” God does not depend on any one person. The second is personal responsibility. God may not need Esther, but he has placed her where she is, and she will answer for what she does with her position. Esther replied with the words that have given courage to many since: “and if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16, ASV).

The ten Booms were not queens. Their position was a watch shop, a narrow house, and a wide circle of friends and customers. But the same logic applied. God did not need them in order to save his people. And yet he had placed them in Haarlem, in that house, at that time, with that century of prayer behind them. Who knew whether they had come to the Beje for such a time as this?

The Cost of Silence

It should be said honestly that most Dutch Christians did not do what the ten Booms did. The churches did protest publicly against the deportations in 1942, and some church leaders were courageous. Thousands of ordinary Dutch people hid Jews at great risk, and many of them paid with their lives. But the great majority kept their heads down and hoped the storm would pass. That was understandable. The penalties for helping Jews were severe, the risks to one’s own family were real, and the occupation lasted five long years. Most of us, if we are honest, would probably have done the same.

That is exactly why the ten Booms matter. They were not unusual people. They were an elderly watchmaker and his two middle-aged daughters, with a son and a married daughter nearby, all of them devout, ordinary, and a little old-fashioned. What set them apart was not strength or cleverness or resources. It was a settled conviction that the lives of their Jewish neighbours were their responsibility before God, and a willingness to act on it when the time came.

For Reflection

The occupation of the Netherlands did not arrive with a single dramatic choice. It crept in step by step, and at each step it was easier to comply than to resist. The measures against the Jews came the same way, one decree at a time, each only a little worse than the last.

That is often how evil works. It rarely asks us to do something monstrous all at once. It asks us to accept one small injustice, then another, and to keep quiet. The question Mordecai put to Esther is one every Christian faces sooner or later, in some form: if we hold our peace at this time, what will we answer for? And who knows whether we have been placed where we are for such a time as this?

fields.title: The First Knock
fields.body_html:
“Deliver them that are carried away unto death, And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back.”

— Proverbs 24:11, ASV

How It Began

No one decided, on a particular day, to turn the Beje into a centre of the Dutch underground. It happened the way most rescue work in occupied Europe happened: one request at a time, each a little larger than the last, until the family found themselves deeply committed to something they had never planned.

The independent sources give the outline. The museum’s chronology says that Corrie and Betsie began helping Jews in 1941 and 1942, at first by finding them places to hide in other people’s homes. The Dutch women’s biographical lexicon says Corrie joined the organised resistance early in 1942. One account dates the first Jewish refugee at the Beje to May 1942, the month the yellow star was introduced. Hiding people in the house itself on a regular basis seems to have begun in the spring of 1943. The first permanent guest, a university student named Hans Poley, arrived in May 1943. That spring many Dutch students went into hiding rather than submit to the occupiers’ demands on the universities.

Corrie’s own accounts fill in the human detail. In her telling, the first refugees came to the door by word of mouth. They were Jews who had been warned that they were about to be picked up, or whose hiding places had become unsafe, and who had heard that the watchmaker’s family would help. The family took them in for a night or two, fed them, and then went looking for somewhere safer for them to go. It soon became clear that finding places was the hard part. It was relatively easy to shelter someone for a night. It was very hard to find a family willing to hide a stranger for months or years, knowing that discovery meant prison or death for the whole household.

A Knock at Night

Corrie’s 1945 book gives a glimpse of what one such night felt like. A Jewish couple, warned that they had been betrayed and that the police were coming, fled to the Beje with nothing, still grieving the possessions they had left behind. The family took them in, and Casper sat with them, because he was good at comforting frightened people. But the house was already full, and a young helper spent the evening walking the town in vain looking for another address. That night, Corrie wrote, the household took one more burden to God in its evening prayers. A place was found two days later.

A Clearing House

By 1943 the Beje had become more than a place where a few people were hidden. It was a hub. The Yad Vashem file on the family records that around eighty resistance workers from several groups visited the house regularly. Corrie described her little room upstairs as a kind of exchange, where the needs of one person were matched with the help another could give.

The needs were endless and varied. There were hiding places to find for children, papers to obtain, and messages to carry to distant provinces. On one occasion, she recorded, a group caring for hundreds of Jewish children asked her help in placing several children who needed psychiatric care, and she arranged for a doctor’s report so that they could be admitted to suitable institutions. It was work that called for a good memory, a wide acquaintance, and the organising skill she had learned running girls’ clubs.

The ten Booms were part of a much larger network. The most important national organisation helping people in hiding was the Landelijke Organisatie voor Hulp aan Onderduikers, the national organisation for help to people in hiding, usually called the LO. It supplied ration cards and papers, often obtained in raids on the distribution offices. The Beje was one node in a web of such groups. Corrie was one of hundreds of people doing similar work across the country, most of them never recognised.

Nollie’s Arrest

The danger was never far away. In 1943 Corrie’s sister Nollie, who lived with her husband and children in another part of Haarlem, was arrested for hiding a Jewish woman in her home. The Yad Vashem file confirms that Nollie was arrested, and that the police warned Corrie. Everyone at the Beje who was at risk moved to other addresses for a time.

The Hiding Place tells the story more fully, and makes it a moral drama. As Corrie tells it, Nollie had a principle of never telling a lie, even to the occupiers. When the police came and asked whether the woman in her house was Jewish, she said yes. The woman was taken. But she was later spirited away from the holding centre in Amsterdam by the underground, and Nollie herself was released after some weeks. In Corrie’s retelling, Nollie’s refusal to lie became a question that troubled the whole family. The next chapter will return to it. Here it is enough to say that this detailed version appears only in the 1971 book, not in the 1945 account, and that the independent record confirms only the arrest and the warning.

“Deliver Them That Are Carried Away unto Death”

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the book of Proverbs: “Deliver them that are carried away unto death, And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back” (Proverbs 24:11, ASV). The next verse anticipates the excuse that most of us would make: “If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this; Doth not he that weigheth the hearts consider it?” (Proverbs 24:12, ASV).

That is precisely the situation of occupied Europe in 1942 and 1943. People really were being carried away to death, and in the Netherlands they were carried away on regular trains from Westerbork. Many Dutch people could tell themselves that they did not know exactly where the trains went or what happened at the end of the line. But Proverbs does not accept that excuse. God, who weighs the heart, knows whether we did not know, or did not want to know.

The ten Booms knew enough. They did not know the full extent of the death camps, which few people in the West understood until later. But they knew that Jews were being hunted and taken away, and that they did not come back. They knew that Scripture told them to deliver those carried away to death. They acted on what they knew.

For Reflection

The ten Booms did not set out to join the resistance. They opened their door to one frightened person, and then another, and each act of help led to the next. By the time they realised how deeply they were involved, there was no going back.

That is often how God leads people into costly obedience. He rarely shows us the whole road at the beginning. He shows us the next person at the door. The question for most of us is not whether we would hide Jews from the Gestapo. It is whether we will open the door to the next person God sends, whoever they are, even when we cannot see where it will lead.

In 1943 Corrie’s sister Nollie, who lived with her husband and children in another part of Haarlem, was arrested for hiding a Jewish woman in her home. The Yad Vashem file confirms that Nollie was arrested, and that the police warned Corrie. Everyone at the Beje who was at risk moved to other addresses for a time. The Hiding Place tells the story more fully, and makes it a moral drama. As Corrie tells it, Nollie had a principle of never telling a lie, even to the occupiers. When the police came and asked whether the woman in her house was Jewish, she said yes. The woman was taken. But she was later spirited away from the holding centre in Amsterdam by the underground, and Nollie herself was released after some weeks. Here it is enough to say that this detailed version appears only in the 1971 book, not in the 1945 account, and that the independent record confirms only the arrest and the warning. “Deliver Them That Are Carried Away unto Death” The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the book of Proverbs: “Deliver them that are carried away unto death, And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back” (Proverbs 24:11, ASV).
