That is precisely the situation of occupied Europe in 1942 and 1943. People really were being carried away to death, and in the Netherlands they were carried away on regular trains from Westerbork. Many Dutch people could tell themselves that they did not know exactly where the trains went or what happened at the end of the line. But Proverbs does not accept that excuse. God, who weighs the heart, knows whether we did not know, or did not want to know. The ten Booms knew enough. They did not know the full extent of the death camps, which few people in the West understood until later. But they knew that Jews were being hunted and taken away, and that they did not come back. They knew that Scripture told them to deliver those carried away to death. They acted on what they knew. For Reflection The ten Booms did not set out to join the resistance. They opened their door to one frightened person, and then another, and each act of help led to the next. By the time they realised how deeply they were involved, there was no going back. That is often how God leads people into costly obedience. He rarely shows us the whole road at the beginning. He shows us the next person at the door. The question for most of us is not whether we would hide Jews from the Gestapo. It is whether we will open the door to the next person God sends, whoever they are, even when we cannot see where it will lead.

fields.title: Ration Cards and Lies
fields.body_html:
“But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive.”

— Exodus 1:17, ASV

The Problem of Food

Hiding a person is not only a matter of a secret room. A person in hiding has to eat, every day, for as long as the hiding lasts. In the occupied Netherlands, that was the hardest problem of all.

Food and many other goods were rationed. Every legal resident received a ration card, and with it coupons that had to be handed over, with money, to buy bread, butter, meat, sugar, and much else. A person in hiding had no legal existence, and so no ration card. A family hiding three or four people had to feed them out of their own rations, which were barely enough for themselves, or buy on the black market at ruinous prices. For a few days that was possible. For months or years, it was not.

The underground’s answer was to obtain ration cards illegally, in large numbers, and distribute them to the people and families who needed them. The national organisation for help to people in hiding, the LO, did much of this work. Many cards came from armed raids on the distribution offices where they were stored, carried out by resistance groups. Others were supplied quietly by sympathetic officials, or forged.

The ten Booms became one of the distribution points. Corrie’s 1945 account describes the steady traffic: “Twenty more ration cards? Right, you shall have them.” She kept a stock of cards hidden inside the top step of the staircase, which had been made into a secret cupboard. No one, she wrote, would ever suspect it was there. In The Hiding Place she tells how the family first obtained cards in quantity through a civil servant at the local food office, a friend she calls Fred Koornstra. As she tells it, he arranged for a hundred cards to be taken from his own office. The name may be a pseudonym, and the story rests on her account. But the Yad Vashem file confirms the essential point: Corrie went on supplying ration cards to Jews hidden in other homes, and she checked those homes in person.

Papers and Names

Food was one problem. Identity was another. Every adult in the occupied Netherlands had to carry an identity card, and Jews’ cards were stamped with a large J. A Jew in hiding who needed to move from one address to another needed false papers. Young men of military age needed permits, called Ausweise, to avoid being sent to Germany as forced labourers. The underground forged, stole, and adapted documents on a large scale, and the Beje was one of the places where such papers passed from hand to hand.

Even names became part of the deception. Corrie’s 1945 account mentions casually that a new guest was given a new name as soon as she arrived. The family called her Tante Mien. The Jewish cantor who became one of the permanent guests is known to history by the nickname the household gave him, Eusie. The name of the civil servant who supplied the cards, the name of the architect who built the hiding place, and many of the young workers who passed through the house are known to us only by aliases. That was deliberate. What you did not know, you could not reveal under interrogation.

The Question of Lying

All of this raised a question that troubled many Christians in the resistance, and troubled the ten Boom family itself. Was it right to lie?

The underground ran on deception. It needed false papers, false names, stolen cards, and hidden rooms, and when the police came to the door, the answers were false. The ninth commandment says, “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor” (Exodus 20:16, ASV). Paul tells the Ephesians, “Wherefore, putting away falsehood, speak ye truth each one with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4:25, ASV). Christians have long argued about whether any lie can ever be justified, even to save a life.

We saw in the last chapter that Corrie’s sister Nollie, as Corrie tells it, would not lie. When the police asked whether the woman in her house was Jewish, Nollie said yes. In The Hiding Place, Corrie presents this as a question on which the family did not agree. Nollie held that God honours those who speak the truth. Corrie did not share her sister’s scruple. The work demanded deception, and she practised it. The Jewish woman whom Nollie refused to deny was, in the end, rescued. Corrie tells the story with evident respect for her sister, but she does not claim to have settled the question.

The Midwives and Rahab

Scripture does not settle it simply either, and it is worth looking at the passages that Christians in the resistance often turned to.

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the beginning of Exodus. Pharaoh had ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill every boy born to the Israelite women. “But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive” (Exodus 1:17, ASV). When Pharaoh demanded to know why, they told him that the Hebrew women gave birth too quickly, before the midwives could arrive. The text does not comment on whether that answer was true. But it says plainly what God thought of the midwives: “And God dealt well with the midwives … And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them households” (Exodus 1:20-21, ASV).

Then there is Rahab of Jericho, who hid the two Israelite spies on her roof. When the king’s messengers came asking for them, she told them the men had already left the city, and sent the pursuers off in the wrong direction (Joshua 2:4-5). The New Testament twice holds her up as an example of faith. “By faith Rahab the harlot perished not with them that were disobedient, having received the spies with peace” (Hebrews 11:31, ASV). James asks, “was not also Rahab the harlot justified by works, in that she received the messengers, and sent them out another way?” (James 2:25, ASV).

Some Christians read these passages as teaching that deception is right when it is used to protect innocent life from murderers. Others read them more cautiously. They say that God rewarded the midwives’ and Rahab’s faith and courage in protecting life, without approving everything they said. Augustine of Hippo, whose works are in this library, held that a Christian must never lie, even to save a life, though he honoured the mercy behind such acts. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, also in this library, wrote an essay in a Nazi prison in 1943 asking what it really means to tell the truth when the one asking the question has no right to the answer. The ten Booms stood in the middle of that argument, and they did not all come down in the same place.

What Was Clear

Whatever one concludes about lying, some things were clear to the ten Booms, and they are clear in Scripture. The occupiers’ laws requiring the registration, marking, and deportation of Jews were unjust, and no one was obliged to help carry them out. “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29, ASV), said Peter and the apostles when they were ordered to stop preaching. The lives of the hunted were precious to God, and those who were able to protect them were responsible for doing so. And those who took these risks did not do so for gain. The ten Booms made no money from the work, and they lost almost everything because of it.

It is also worth noticing that, in Corrie’s telling, the disagreement did not break the family’s unity or its work. Paul’s counsel to the Romans about disputed matters applies here: “Let each man be fully assured in his own mind” (Romans 14:5, ASV). In a crisis, Christians of good faith may reach different conclusions about hard questions. What matters is that they act before God, in love, and with a clear conscience.

For Reflection

Most of us will never have to decide whether to lie to the secret police. But the question behind the ten Booms’ argument is not remote. How do we hold together the command to be truthful and the command to protect the vulnerable? And how do we disagree with fellow Christians about hard questions without breaking fellowship?

The midwives in Egypt did not write a treatise on ethics. They feared God more than Pharaoh, and they saved the children. That, at least, is clear. In an unjust world, fearing God more than the powers of the age will sometimes mean refusing to cooperate with evil, at real cost to ourselves. The ten Booms learned that lesson in a watch shop in Haarlem. They were still learning it when the Gestapo came.

fields.title: The Angels’ Crib
fields.body_html:
“Thou art my hiding-place; thou wilt preserve me from trouble; Thou wilt compass me about with songs of deliverance.”

— Psalm 32:7, ASV

An Architect Called Smit

By the spring of 1943 it was clear that the Beje needed more than good intentions. People were living in the house for weeks and months, and at any moment the police might come to the door. A raid by the Sicherheitsdienst, the SS security service, often came without warning, and there would be only a minute or two to hide. The family needed a hiding place that could not be found.

The man who built it is known only by an alias. In The Hiding Place Corrie calls him Mr. Smit, a well-known architect who worked for the underground and came to the Beje to survey the house. The Dutch regional history of the house says he was found through a local resistance man named Herman Sluring, whom Corrie’s book calls “Pickwick.” The architect’s real name has never been established, and the museum does not give it. He belongs to the large company of people in the Dutch resistance whose work survives and whose names do not.

According to the museum and the Dutch sources, the hiding place was built in the spring or early summer of 1943. The architect chose Corrie’s own bedroom, at the very top of the house. It was the highest point, farthest from the street door, which gave precious seconds of warning. Along one wall of the room he built a second wall of brick, plastered and aged to look exactly like the original, with a narrow space between the two. The Dutch war-graves foundation, which maintains the memorial at the house, gives the space as about two and a half metres long and seventy centimetres deep. Against the new wall stood a linen cupboard. Under its bottom shelf was a small sliding panel. A person could crawl through the panel into the space behind, and the panel could be closed from inside and hidden with boxes and linen.

The family called it the Engelenbak, the “Angels’ Crib.” It was the highest seat in an old Dutch theatre, the gallery nearest the angels. It was not a place to live. It had no light and no room to sit comfortably for long. There was a grille for a little air, a mattress on the floor, a supply of water, and some dry biscuits. It was meant to hide people for hours, not days. In the event, six people would stand in it for two and a half days.

Drills with a Stopwatch

A hiding place is useless if people cannot reach it in time, so the household practised. A system of buzzers had been installed so that a warning could be given from the shop. Corrie would sound the alarm without notice, often at night, and time the guests with a stopwatch as they raced upstairs, hid every trace of themselves, and crawled one by one through the panel. Their best time, she recorded in 1945, was seventy seconds. Afterwards they went over whatever had given them away, and Corrie rewarded everyone with cream puffs, which made the drills almost something to look forward to.

It is a tender picture, and a terrible one. Grown men and women were rehearsing how to vanish into a wall in the middle of the night, because they were being hunted. The cream puffs were Corrie’s way of making the unbearable bearable.

The Guests

Over the months, Corrie wrote in 1945, more than eighty people passed through the Beje for shorter or longer stays. There were never fewer than seven and never more than twelve in the house at one time. A small group stayed permanently, and some of them can now be identified from the independent record.

“Eusie” was Meijer Mossel, a cantor from the Jewish community of Amsterdam, a man with a fine voice and, as Corrie remembered him, the high spirits of an overgrown boy. “Mary” was Margaretha Jacqueline van Itallie, born in Leiden in 1900, who had run a travel agency before the war. She taught Italian to the household in the evenings. “Thea,” named in Corrie’s later book, has been identified by Yad Vashem as a nurse named Hansje Frankfort-Israels. Hans Poley was the student who had arrived in May 1943 as the first permanent guest. He later wrote his own memoir of the house, drawing on his wartime diaries. Corrie’s nephew Peter van Woerden, Nollie’s son, a gifted young musician, was often there. So were young resistance workers such as Reynout Siertsema. Other names that appear in Corrie’s books, such as Martha, Henk, Leendert, and Meta, have not been identified independently, and may be pseudonyms or first names only.

“The Gayest Underground Address”

What stands out in Corrie’s earliest account is not the fear but the life. Her first chapter opens with music in the drawing room: a violin sonata played by a young man in hiding, and Eusie singing so passionately that Corrie had to warn him the whole street would hear. People said, she recorded, that the Beje was the gayest underground address in the Netherlands.

The household held its own evening classes. Mary taught Italian, Eusie Hebrew, and Hans astronomy, and old Casper, well into his eighties, came to learn with the rest. The family cat bore the grand biblical name Maher-shalal-hash-baz, from Isaiah 8:1. There were jokes, music, and even a pretended birthday party when a window cleaner’s ladder appeared unexpectedly at the window. Under the laughter, Corrie knew that sooner or later the house would be discovered, and she kept a small Bible about her person against that day.

“Thou Art My Hiding-Place”

The verse at the head of this chapter is from Psalm 32: “Thou art my hiding-place; thou wilt preserve me from trouble; Thou wilt compass me about with songs of deliverance” (Psalm 32:7, ASV). The psalm is David’s song of a forgiven sinner who has found in God a refuge from the storm. “Surely when the great waters overflow they shall not reach unto him” (Psalm 32:6, ASV).

The Angels’ Crib was a real hiding place, and a well-made one. It would do exactly what it was built to do. But the household knew that no wall of brick could finally protect them. They practised their drills and trusted God, and they did not confuse the two. The Beje was, in Corrie’s phrase, full of songs, violin sonatas and Jewish chants and hymns and birthday songs, even while its guests practised vanishing into a wall. “Thou wilt compass me about with songs of deliverance.” The songs came first. The deliverance, for most of them, would come later, and by a harder road than any of them imagined.

For Reflection

The Beje in 1943 held two things at once: careful, practical preparation for disaster, and a stubborn, joyful life in the meantime. The household drilled with a stopwatch, and it also held classes, concerts, and cream-puff suppers. It did not deny the danger, and it did not let the danger have the last word.

That is a good pattern for Christian life under pressure. We are to be wise and prepared, and to do the practical things that love requires. But we are also to live joyfully, because our final hiding place is not a wall we have built. It is God himself.

The household drilled with a stopwatch, and it also held classes, concerts, and cream-puff suppers. It did not deny the danger, and it did not let the danger have the last word. That is a good pattern for Christian life under pressure. We are to be wise and prepared, and to do the practical things that love requires. But we are also to live joyfully, because our final hiding place is not a wall we have built. It is God himself.

fields.title: 28 February 1944
fields.body_html:
“He that dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High Shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of Jehovah, He is my refuge and my fortress; My God, in whom I trust.”

— Psalm 91:1-2, ASV

Monday Morning

On Monday, 28 February 1944, Corrie ten Boom was in bed with influenza. Downstairs her brother Willem was leading a Bible study, and the house was busier than usual. When the alarm sounded, four Jewish guests and two young resistance workers carrying incriminating papers ran past her bed into the hiding place. Corrie pushed her own records in after them, hid the panel, and was back in bed when the raiders reached the top of the stairs.

The raid was carried out by the Sicherheitsdienst, the German security police, with officers of the Haarlem police. That much is confirmed by the Dutch war-graves foundation and the museum.

“Where Is Your Secret Room?”

Corrie was arrested at once. When she refused to reveal the hiding place, she was told the house would simply be watched until whoever was inside gave themselves up. Downstairs, everyone who had come to the Bible study, and everyone who arrived during the day, was detained as they walked in. The house had become a trap.

The officer in charge, whom Corrie later called Kapteyn, questioned her in the shop and struck her repeatedly across the face. When she cried out to Jesus to protect her, he threatened her life, and then stopped. Betsie was beaten too. Afterwards, Corrie recorded, Betsie said that she pitied the man who had done it. The house was searched and the family’s savings and some valuables were taken. But the searchers did not find the Angels’ Crib.

“Jesus Is Victor”

For hours the prisoners waited in the dining room in silence. The telephone kept ringing with warnings from friends, and Corrie had to answer under a guard’s eye. Before long the line went dead, and the warning began to spread.

On the fireplace hung a small wooden plaque with the words “Jesus is Victor.” Betsie drew Corrie’s attention to it, and their father said aloud that it was true. It looked, Corrie thought, as though the Gestapo had won, and they had not. She did not understand what was happening, and she knew that believing is not the same as understanding.

When one of the Germans, noticing a Bible, asked the old man what it said about the government, Casper answered with Peter’s words about fearing God and honouring the Queen. As he was led out, he thought of the old clock in the hall that needed winding.

A Night at the Police Station

The prisoners were taken to the police station in the Smedestraat. How many were arrested that day is uncertain. The Dutch war-graves foundation and a regional history give twenty-one. The museum, Yad Vashem, and the Holocaust encyclopedia say more than thirty. Corrie counted thirty-five at the police station. The difference probably comes from people who walked into the trap later in the day. It is safest to say that some two or three dozen people were taken.

At the station a large mattress was put on the floor for the family. Casper lay down on it with all his children and one grandson around him: Betsie, Corrie, Nollie, Willem, and Nollie’s son Peter. Betsie remarked that she had once seen this very scene in a dream, their father and all his children lying on a mattress, without understanding it. Before they slept, Casper gathered them round him. At his request Willem read the ninety-first Psalm, and then the old man prayed. It was the last time, Corrie wrote, that she would hear her father pray.

The psalm Willem read that night is the one at the head of this chapter. “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High Shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of Jehovah, He is my refuge and my fortress; My God, in whom I trust” (Psalm 91:1-2, ASV). It goes on to promise that God will deliver his people from the snare of the fowler, and that they need not be afraid of the terror by night. It is a psalm of protection, and the family read it on the night that protection seemed to have failed. They were not naive. Casper was eighty-four and ill, and they all knew what prison might mean for him. But the psalm’s deepest promise is not that nothing bad will happen. It is that God himself is the refuge. “He shall call upon me, and I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble” (Psalm 91:15, ASV).

Corrie also recorded that one of the men arrested with them was in fact a planted informer, and that they were warned in time.

The next day the prisoners were loaded onto a bus for Scheveningen, the seaside suburb of The Hague where the Germans held political prisoners. Corrie remembered the people of Haarlem standing silently along the street as they left, many of them in tears. The town, she wrote, loved her father and called him its grand old man. The sun shone on the Grote Kerk. It was, she thought, a bright last greeting from Haarlem.

Two and a Half Days in the Wall

Behind the false wall in Corrie’s bedroom, six people stood in the dark. There were four Jews and two resistance workers. The Germans were sure they were in the house, and left guards inside to wait for them to come out. The six stood from Monday afternoon until Wednesday. The hiding place had no room to lie down properly, very little air, and almost nothing to eat or drink.

On Wednesday, 1 March, policemen sympathetic to the resistance came on duty at the house. The museum names two of them, Jan Overzet and Theo Ederveen. Word had reached them, through the underground, of the people trapped in the wall, and when it was safe they let them out. The two resistance workers left over the neighbouring roofs. The Jews waited until dark and then left by a side door. Corrie’s 1945 account adds a detail she must have heard later. Eusie was so glad to be outside that he raised his arms in the middle of the street and chanted a Jewish prayer.

In prison, as she later told it in The Hiding Place, Corrie received a smuggled message that all the watches in her cupboard were safe. She understood. The hiding place had held.

What Became of the Six

Many retellings of Corrie’s story stop there, as though all six people were saved. The truth is harder, and they deserve to have it told.

The Jewish memorial register of the Netherlands records that Mary van Itallie, the travel agent who had taught Italian at the Beje, was arrested again within days at the new address where she had been placed. She was sent to the transit camp at Westerbork and on 23 March 1944 put on a train to Auschwitz. She died there on 1 May 1944. The Yad Vashem file’s statement that the Jews from the hiding place remained hidden for the rest of the war is not correct.

Meijer Mossel, the cantor Eusie, went into hiding in Friesland in the north. He too was eventually betrayed and arrested, and reached Westerbork in January 1945. By then the trains to the east had stopped, and he survived. After the war he became a well-known cantor. The museum says that one of the Jews and one of the resistance workers did not survive. The Dutch war-graves foundation says that three of the six survived. The sources do not agree, and the full fate of every one of the six has not been established.

Who Betrayed Them?

The question of the informer belongs here too, and it also needs careful telling.

The Hiding Place tells how on the morning of the raid a man came to the shop and asked Corrie for money to bribe the police to release his wife, who had been arrested for hiding Jews. She gave him money. In the 1971 book he is the informer, and he is named as Jan Vogel. But this scene does not appear in Corrie’s 1945 account, which does not say how the house was betrayed. A Dutch local historian gives the name differently, as H. van Vogel. The museum says the informer was sentenced to death after the war and executed. But the list of people executed under Dutch postwar special justice contains no one of that name. Many death sentences were commuted, and without the court records, which are not public, his fate cannot be settled. What is documented is that Corrie wrote to him in June 1945 to tell him she forgave him. That letter belongs to a later chapter.

For Reflection

On 28 February 1944 the Beje’s hiding place did what it was built to do. The house did not protect those who built it. Casper, Betsie, Corrie, and their friends went to prison, and not everyone who stood in the wall that day survived the war.

That is a sober ending to the story of the hiding place, and it is the true one. Psalm 91 does not promise that believers will be spared all harm. The people who read it on the police-station mattress that night would soon learn how much harm could come. But it promises that God will be with his people in trouble. The rest of Corrie’s story is about how that promise held when every human hiding place had failed.

fields.title: “Father Was Released”
fields.body_html:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.”

— Psalm 27:10, ASV

The Last Glimpse

From Haarlem the prisoners were driven to the German security offices in The Hague, and then to the prison at Scheveningen on the coast. The Dutch came to call it the Oranjehotel, the Orange Hotel, because so many loyal patriots were held there. Casper was so frail that the guards had to carry him. Corrie remembered an officer calling him the worst of them all, because he spoke of nothing but Jesus and the Queen. Inside the gate, father and daughter exchanged a blessing, and she looked back at him once. She never saw him again.

The Dutch war-graves foundation records that Casper ten Boom died in The Hague on 9 March 1944, nine days after his arrest. The accounts of where he died differ. The foundation’s records mention the Scheveningen prison and a clinic in the district of Loosduinen. Corrie was later told that his mind had become confused, and that he died in a hospital corridor. His fellow prisoners reported that he stayed brave to the end, saying that if he were freed he would go straight back to helping the Jews. He was buried in a pauper’s grave. After the war his remains were moved to the national cemetery of honour at Loenen.

His children, several of them in the same prison, were not told. Relatives who went to The Hague to ask after him eventually learned, after being passed from office to office, that he had already been buried.

A Martyr’s Death

When the news reached Betsie, she wrote home that she had always expected their father to die a martyr’s death rather than in his bed. Casper had once said that he would count it an honour to give his life for God’s ancient people. Corrie’s 1945 book notes simply that the honour had now been given him. A grandchild’s note to Betsie in prison put the family’s comfort in his own words: the best had come for him at last.

The psalm at the head of this chapter was written for moments like this. “When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up” (Psalm 27:10, ASV). Casper had not forsaken his daughters. He had been taken from them, and they had not been allowed to be with him when he died. The psalmist’s promise is that there is a Father who is never taken away. The same psalm begins, “Jehovah is my light and my salvation; Whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 27:1, ASV), and it contains a line that Corrie would come to know well: “For in the day of trouble he will keep me secretly in his pavilion: In the covert of his tabernacle will he hide me” (Psalm 27:5, ASV).

A Crowded Cell

Corrie spent her first days in a crowded cell with women of very different backgrounds, still sick with the influenza she had caught before the raid. In the second week she was taken under guard to a doctor, who diagnosed pleurisy. A nurse there quietly asked how she could help, and managed to slip Corrie some small booklets of the Gospels. Corrie never forgot the kindness.

Solitary

Soon afterwards she was moved into solitary confinement, and there she stayed for weeks. Her 1945 account of that time is honest about fear and loneliness. The cell was cold and grey, she was ill, and at first she longed for any human face. The guards were hard, and punished her for asking about her father and for singing. She went on singing anyway.

Small things kept her going. She befriended a line of ants on the floor and fed them crumbs. She embroidered her prison clothes with threads from a coloured towel sent from home. When she was finally let out alone into the prison garden, she felt at first overwhelmed by colour, and then by the menace of the place. A verse steadied her: “And Enoch walked with God” (Genesis 5:24, ASV). She was not walking alone either.

A Letter from Nollie

At last a letter arrived from Nollie, who had been released. It told her, gently, that their father had lived only ten days after his arrest. Corrie wept for the first time since the raid. The guard she called for offered little comfort, only the suggestion that it was her own fault for breaking the law. Corrie recalled the proverb: “The tender mercies of the wicked are cruel” (Proverbs 12:10, ASV).

Her letters home in the following weeks show her working through her grief. She wrote that her father’s death left a great emptiness, and that the love and care she had given him would find another outlet.

The Lieutenant

Some weeks into her imprisonment Corrie was interrogated. Hearings were the terror of the prison, and she had been rehearsed for one by the young people of the underground, who had even questioned her in the night for practice. She gave away no names.

The officer, whom The Hiding Place names as Lieutenant Rahms, surprised her by his courtesy. When he learned of her classes for disabled people, he asked whether such work was not a waste of time. Corrie recognised the question as the voice of the regime, and answered that God’s love reaches especially the weak and despised, and that in God’s eyes such a person might be worth more than either of them. The next day, she recorded, he told her he had not slept for thinking about what she had said, and confided the darkness of his own life, with a family in a bombed German city whose fate he did not know. Corrie told him that there was no darkness Jesus could not dispel.

The statement he drew up, as she remembered it, recorded that she meant to go on helping anyone who needed it, “regardless of their race or creed,” because she was following Christ’s command to love God and her neighbour. We have it only as she remembered it, written down within a year.

Betsie’s questioning lasted several days, and each session, by the officer’s leave, ended in prayer. Nearly everyone arrested with them was released after questioning. Corrie, Betsie, and one of the young men remained.

The Watches Are Safe

In The Hiding Place Corrie tells how she received a message in prison, hidden in a parcel, that all the watches in her cupboard were safe. She understood at once. The six people in the hiding place had not been found. The message brought her great joy. She could not know then what we know now: that not all of the six would survive the war.

For Reflection

The weeks in solitary confinement at Scheveningen were, in some ways, the loneliest of Corrie’s life. She had lost her home and her father, and she was separated from her sister. She was sick, cold, and alone. Yet her 1945 account also records a closeness to God she had never known before. Never before, she wrote, had fellowship with him been so near.

Many people who have gone through suffering say something similar. God does not always remove the loneliness. But he comes into it. “When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.”

fields.title: Vught
fields.body_html:
“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned, neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.”

— Isaiah 43:2, ASV

Together Again

On 6 June 1944, the day Allied forces landed in Normandy, the Germans began emptying the prison at Scheveningen. Rumours of invasion had run through the cells all day. The prisoners were ordered to put on their own clothes and pack their belongings. After hours of waiting they were loaded into buses and vans, and taken to a small station outside The Hague. There, among the crowd of prisoners, Corrie saw Betsie for the first time in more than three months.

They pushed through the crowd until they were in the same railway carriage, and sat side by side, holding hands, hardly needing to speak. One of the other women teased them as “the love-birds.” They had lived together, Corrie wrote, for more than fifty years in almost perfect harmony, and now, after months apart, they were together again. Whatever came next, they would face it side by side.

The train arrived at four in the morning at Vught, near ‘s-Hertogenbosch in the south of the Netherlands. It was a concentration camp the Germans called Herzogenbusch, the only SS concentration camp built on Dutch soil. The prisoners were driven through the darkness by soldiers with levelled guns, under searchlights, through a wood.

Answered Prayer

Corrie’s account of the first day at Vught records a small deliverance she always counted as answered prayer. The women were being made to undress and shower in front of watching soldiers, and the two sisters held each other and prayed to be spared. Before their turn came, the procedure was halted, and when they were processed days later it was done privately. God answers prayers, Corrie wrote.

A Society for Not Grumbling

The women from Scheveningen were first kept apart from the main camp, in a single large barracks where they sat all day at long tables with nothing to do. Boredom set in, and with it complaining and backbiting. Betsie had an idea. She founded a society, as the Dutch always seem to do, with simple rules. Members promised to do their best not to grumble or complain, not to speak ill of anyone, and to speak encouragingly to others. They also resolved to obey the orders of the prisoners put in charge of them. A small group met daily to pray that the atmosphere would improve.

It is a very Betsie idea: small, practical, gentle, and rooted in prayer. It reflects Paul’s counsel to the Philippians: “Do all things without murmurings and questionings; that ye may become blameless and harmless, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom ye are seen as lights in the world” (Philippians 2:14-15, ASV).

One day the sisters were called out and given forms that other prisoners said meant release. They gave away their few possessions, said goodbye, and collected their watches and rings from the camp office, already imagining the journey home. Instead they were kept waiting for hours at the camp exit, among men who warned them that they were more likely bound for the punishment cells, and beside a Jewish woman who had just been singled out and made to stand facing the wall. Corrie prayed for God’s ancient people. Betsie, whose heart was beating irregularly, said that evidently the Lord still had work for them there, and began to sing.

In the end the threat passed. They were not put in the bunkers, and that evening they were marched instead into the main camp at Vught, where a young prisoner welcomed them to her table.

The Watchmaker at the Workbench

In the main camp most of the women worked for the Philips electronics company, which ran workshops at Vught using prison labour. Corrie was lined up with other older women to be inspected by the men in charge of the work crews. It felt, she wrote, like a slave market. She thought of Jesus’ words to Peter: “another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not” (John 21:18, ASV). She had always been independent. Now she was being humbled, and she told herself that she was “in training.”

She was sent to a workshop where the foreman, a fellow prisoner who had been a headmaster, ran the room with courtesy and care. At first she measured small glass rods. When the foreman noticed her interest in the more intricate work and learned that she was a watchmaker, he moved her to testing relay switches for radios. It was precise work, she wrote, but not as interesting as repairing watches. She worked eleven hours a day. When officers approached, someone at the window would call out a code word, and books, letters, and handwork would vanish. Betsie worked in the sewing room.

It was in some ways, Corrie admitted, much more bearable than solitary confinement. There was fresh air and sunlight, the great skies of Brabant, and friendship with other prisoners, some of them remarkable people. But it was still a concentration camp. Men were beaten to death. Prisoners were called out of the ranks at roll-call and shot a few minutes later. Corrie heard the volleys from the bunkers at night, and learned to pray then for the bereaved and for those who might be next.

A Church on the Grass

On Sunday afternoons the prisoners had some free time. On the first Sunday a girl invited the sisters to a worship service on a patch of grass between two barracks, where a woman was reading from the Bible. Corrie was asked to lead the prayer of thanksgiving, and the next week to lead the whole service. She began a discussion group in the evenings, as she used to do in her girls’ clubs, to lift the women’s thinking beyond the barbed wire.

The questions she prepared have survived in her 1945 book, and they are worth noting. They asked what the prisoners’ responsibility would be after the camp: to people who returned to find their families gone, to those who had lost their homes, to those whose minds had been broken, and to young people who would struggle to return to normal life. And one question asked whether they had any responsibilities towards the defeated enemy. In the summer of 1944, in a Nazi concentration camp, Corrie ten Boom was already asking her fellow prisoners how they would treat the Germans after the war. The seed of her life’s later work was already there.

She admitted that as a discussion it was a failure. The women held very different views, and they did not understand one another. But it had lifted their thinking beyond the wire.

How Long?

Letters smuggled out of Vught show the sisters trying to calculate when they would be free. Other prisoners said that six months at Vught was the usual term. Corrie wondered whether their time would end on 1 September, or on 6 September if the weeks at Scheveningen were counted, or on 8 December. These letters matter for the later story of her release. They show that in 1944 the sisters expected their imprisonment to end at a definite date. They did not expect to be held indefinitely.

In the same letters Corrie was frank about herself. Some of the women around her were heroines, she wrote, who had lost everything and made a conscious sacrifice of it. She was not like that. She longed terribly for home and comfort. That she had held out at all was only by God’s grace.

A Hundred and Eighty Shots

By late August 1944 the Allied armies were approaching the Netherlands, and rumours of liberation swept the camp. The prisoners counted the kilometres. Then, in the first days of September, as the front drew near, the Germans began to empty Vught and to kill many of the male prisoners before they could be freed.

Corrie described one of those days. The women crowded at the fence separating them from the men’s camp and watched as men were called out of the ranks and marched out of the gate. The women waited. Then they heard the shots. Corrie counted one hundred and eighty. Every shot, she wrote, meant the death of a good Dutchman, and every woman there wondered whether her husband, fiancé, or son was among them.

Corrie laid her head on Betsie’s shoulder and asked God why he allowed it. Betsie’s face, she noticed, was serene, as though the horror could not reach her. Corrie led her away and poured out her grief to God. She felt that she was told she could not, and need not, carry the sorrows of the whole world herself. She should bring them to him and leave them there. Peace came.

Her 1945 book records the image she found for it that night, an image she would repeat for the rest of her life. Everything in life looks like the back of a piece of embroidery, she wrote, a meaningless tangle of threads. But that is the underside. One day we will see the right side, and be amazed and thankful. The image is often associated with her later preaching and with a poem she liked to quote. It first appears here, at Vught, on the night of the executions.

East

Within days Vught was being evacuated. The sisters knew now that this did not mean freedom. They saw cartloads of files going to the furnaces, and the sick being carried to the train. On about 4 September 1944 they were loaded into a goods wagon with some eighty other women, twice as many as it was meant to hold. There were no windows and almost no air. Some of the women pried holes in the walls with knives until fresh air came through. At one point the train was fired on, in what turned out to be a failed rescue attempt by the resistance. Then it crossed the border into Germany. Someone in another wagon began to sing the old song of farewell to the Netherlands.

The journey lasted three days and three nights. Corrie was ill and tormented by thirst. At last the train stopped at Fürstenberg, a small town north of Berlin, and the women stumbled out and were marched along the shore of a lake. Corrie collapsed on the grass. Looking out over the lake to a church spire and the woods beyond, she thought of the twenty-third psalm: green pastures, still waters, and the valley of the shadow of death. Then they walked on to the gates of Ravensbrück.

For Reflection

The verse at the head of this chapter does not promise that God’s people will avoid the waters and the fire. It promises that he will be with them as they pass through. “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee … when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned” (Isaiah 43:2, ASV).

Vught was a place of both, of small mercies and great horrors. It had friendship at the workbench and executions beyond the wire, a church service on the grass and the sound of volleys in the night. Corrie did not pretend to understand it. What she learned there was the embroidery lesson. We see only the underside now, and one day we will see the pattern. In the meantime, we are not asked to carry the whole world’s grief, only to bring it to the One who can.

fields.title: Barracks 28
fields.body_html:
“in everything give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus to you-ward.”

— 1 Thessalonians 5:18, ASV

Heads Up

Ravensbrück, about eighty kilometres north of Berlin, was the largest concentration camp for women in the Nazi system. Over the six years of its existence well over a hundred thousand women passed through its gates, from every country in Europe. Tens of thousands died there, of hunger, disease, exhaustion, beatings, medical experiments, and, in the final months, in a gas chamber. When Corrie and Betsie arrived in September 1944, the camp was already hugely overcrowded, and growing worse by the week as prisoners were brought in from camps further east.

The Dutch women came through the gate in ranks, still in their overalls from Vught, and some of them were singing. Corrie was astonished that they could. But the first women they passed were skeletons reaching out for bread, and a Dutch prisoner who had been there longer gave her a description of the camp so bleak that she refused at first to believe it. It turned out to be true.

Nights in the Open

For the first nights the new arrivals had no shelter at all, first in a crowded tent full of vermin and then on the open ground. The sisters cut Betsie’s hair short because of the lice. Lying together under one blanket, they comforted each other with the psalms, and Betsie reminded Corrie that God gives his beloved sleep (Psalm 127:2). Then it began to rain.

The Bible Under the Dress

After two nights in the open the newcomers were processed. Everything they had brought, clothes, blankets and food, was taken, and they came out wearing a thin dress and wooden shoes. The sisters prayed first for the strength to give it all up. Then Corrie found a way to keep what mattered most. She hid their woollen underwear and her small Bible in a corner during the showers, put them on again under her dress, and walked past the guards who were searching every prisoner. She was not searched. She believed all her life that God had hidden her, and she wrote that after that she could face even Ravensbrück without fear.

One does not have to share every detail of her interpretation to be moved by the result. Two middle-aged Dutch women entered one of the worst camps in Europe carrying a Bible, and it would be read aloud, day after day, to hundreds of women.

Barracks 28

In the quarantine barracks where they spent their first weeks, Corrie measured the bunks with her hand, as she had taught her club girls to do, and found them about seventy centimetres wide, with several women to each pair. Then the sisters were moved to Barracks 28. It was meant for a few hundred prisoners. Corrie later wrote that by the end it held some fourteen hundred. Windows were broken and stuffed with rags. The bunks, three tiers high, were missing slats, and when the women climbed in, some of the upper ones collapsed, showering straw and filth on those below. Two women, and sometimes more, slept in each narrow bunk. The air was foul, and the place was alive with lice. Barracks 28 was their home for the rest of Betsie’s life.

Here the sisters began the work that Corrie came to believe was the reason they had been sent to Ravensbrück. With their hidden Bible they held Bible readings every day, sometimes twice. Corrie preached, and Betsie prayed and comforted. Corrie wrote that on one Sunday she preached nine times, crawling along the top tier of bunks under the ceiling to groups of young women who had asked her to come. Dutch, Belgian, French, Polish, and Russian women listened, Protestants and Catholics together. When the sisters could not share a language with a Polish or Russian woman, they said only the name of Jesus, and her face would light up. There would be no separate Protestant and Catholic areas in heaven, Corrie reflected, so why should there be any in Ravensbrück?

The Fleas

The best-known story about Barracks 28 is not in Corrie’s 1945 account. It appears in The Hiding Place, published in 1971.

As it is told there, the barracks was infested with fleas, and Corrie complained bitterly. Betsie reminded her of Paul’s command, “in everything give thanks” (1 Thessalonians 5:18, ASV), and insisted that they thank God even for the fleas. Corrie thought this absurd, but joined in. Later they noticed that the guards never came into their part of the barracks, and so the Bible readings could go on undisturbed. They learned why. The guards would not enter because of the fleas.

The 1945 book has a related detail. It says the barracks was full of lice, and that women from other barracks were reluctant to visit because of them. It also says that as the camp became overcrowded, supervision in the barracks grew slack, and the Bible readings could continue without interruption. It does not mention thanking God for the fleas. It is possible that Corrie remembered the fleas and Betsie’s thanksgiving clearly and simply did not include them in 1945. It is also possible that the story took its sharp shape in the retelling. Either way, the lesson it carries was certainly Betsie’s. Her whole life in the camp, as the 1945 book describes it, was an exercise in giving thanks in everything.

Appealing Higher

One more small scene from the 1945 book shows Betsie’s way of seeing things. The women in the quarantine barracks were being driven out to roll-call again and again, all day long, until they were close to collapse. Someone said that one of them must get through to the camp commander and complain. The other women asked Betsie what she thought. No, she said. It would do no good. They must appeal higher, to the Weltführer, the leader of the world. He alone could help them. The women learned later that the commander was a brutal man, and that complaining to him would have been dangerous. They also learned that the endless roll-calls had been deliberately designed to break their spirits.

Roll-Call

Life in Ravensbrück was organised around roll-call. At half past four in the morning, often earlier, tens of thousands of women were driven out into the camp street and made to stand in ranks, in rain, snow, and freezing wind, while they were counted and counted again. It went on for hours. Anyone who moved or collapsed might be beaten. The sick and the dying had to be there too. On one terrible morning the women stood outside for three quarters of an hour after roll-call because the barracks door was locked. A guard beat a woman who tried to get in through a window. A disabled girl who soiled herself was savagely beaten, and an old woman collapsed. Betsie, leaning on Corrie, whispered that this was hell. Corrie whispered back God’s promise never to leave or forsake them (Hebrews 13:5). Then the rising sun caught the clouds from below and turned them red. Corrie thought that the light of the Saviour could shine on them even there, so that they would reflect it. She did not understand it, she wrote. Believing is not seeing.

Red Cards and Sick Transports

The sisters worked for a time in a Siemens factory outside the camp, hauling iron plates in the cold. Betsie was too weak for it. Corrie’s 1945 account tells how, when she was selected for a transport to a munitions factory, a woman doctor helped her stay by pretending that she needed new glasses. Soon afterwards both sisters were placed in a knitting detail, which allowed them to stay in the barracks. That gave Corrie time for the Bible readings.

They were also issued red cards, which marked them as unfit for heavy work. The next morning Corrie heard that when the camp became overcrowded, women with red cards were killed. She also saw, one foggy morning at roll-call, open trucks drawn up outside the hospital barracks. Nurses helped a hundred sick women onto them: the disabled, the incurable, and some who were simply troublesome. The trucks drove away into the mist. Everyone knew there was no return from those transports. The historical record confirms what she saw. In the last months of 1944 and early 1945, Ravensbrück was killing its sick and weak, first by such transports and by selections, and from January 1945 in a gas chamber.

For Reflection

The command at the head of this chapter is one of the hardest in Scripture: “in everything give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus to you-ward” (1 Thessalonians 5:18, ASV). Paul does not say “for everything,” as though evil itself were a gift. He says “in everything,” in every circumstance, however dark.

Betsie ten Boom gave thanks in Barracks 28. Whatever exactly she said about the fleas, she thanked God in a place designed to break human beings. She did not deny the evil around her, and she did not let it have the last word. Most of us will never be tested as she was. But we can practise, in our smaller trials, the discipline of looking for God’s hand in everything, and giving thanks.

Later they noticed that the guards never came into their part of the barracks, and so the Bible readings could go on undisturbed. They learned why. The guards would not enter because of the fleas. The 1945 book has a related detail. It says the barracks was full of lice, and that women from other barracks were reluctant to visit because of them. It also says that as the camp became overcrowded, supervision in the barracks grew slack, and the Bible readings could continue without interruption. It does not mention thanking God for the fleas. It is possible that Corrie remembered the fleas and Betsie’s thanksgiving clearly and simply did not include them in 1945. It is also possible that the story took its sharp shape in the retelling. Either way, the lesson it carries was certainly Betsie’s. Her whole life in the camp, as the 1945 book describes it, was an exercise in giving thanks in everything. Appealing Higher One more small scene from the 1945 book shows Betsie’s way of seeing things. The women in the quarantine barracks were being driven out to roll-call again and again, all day long, until they were close to collapse. Someone said that one of them must get through to the camp commander and complain. The other women asked Betsie what she thought. No, she said. It would do no good. They must appeal higher, to the Weltführer, the leader of the world. He alone could help them. The women learned later that the commander was a brutal man, and that complaining to him would have been dangerous. They also learned that the endless roll-calls had been deliberately designed to break their spirits. Roll-Call Life in Ravensbrück was organised around roll-call. At half past four in the morning, often earlier, tens of thousands of women were driven out into the camp street and made to stand in ranks, in rain, snow, and freezing wind, while they were counted and counted again. It went on for hours. Anyone who moved or collapsed might be beaten. The sick and the dying had to be there too. On one terrible morning the women stood outside for three quarters of an hour after roll-call because the barracks door was locked. A guard beat a woman who tried to get in through a window. A disabled girl who soiled herself was savagely beaten, and an old woman collapsed. Betsie, leaning on Corrie, whispered that this was hell. Corrie whispered back God’s promise never to leave or forsake them (Hebrews 13:5). Then the rising sun caught the clouds from below and turned them red. Corrie thought that the light of the Saviour could shine on them even there, so that they would reflect it. She did not understand it, she wrote. Believing is not seeing. Red Cards and Sick Transports The sisters worked for a time in a Siemens factory outside the camp, hauling iron plates in the cold. Betsie was too weak for it. Corrie’s 1945 account tells how, when she was selected for a transport to a munitions factory, a woman doctor helped her stay by pretending that she needed new glasses. Soon afterwards both sisters were placed in a knitting detail, which allowed them to stay in the barracks. That gave Corrie time for the Bible readings. They were also issued red cards, which marked them as unfit for heavy work. The next morning Corrie heard that when the camp became overcrowded, women with red cards were killed. She also saw, one foggy morning at roll-call, open trucks drawn up outside the hospital barracks. Nurses helped a hundred sick women onto them: the disabled, the incurable, and some who were simply troublesome. The trucks drove away into the mist. Everyone knew there was no return from those transports. The historical record confirms what she saw. In the last months of 1944 and early 1945, Ravensbrück was killing its sick and weak, first by such transports and by selections, and from January 1945 in a gas chamber. For Reflection The command at the head of this chapter is one of the hardest in Scripture: “in everything give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus to you-ward” (1 Thessalonians 5:18, ASV). Paul does not say “for everything,” as though evil itself were a gift. He says “in everything,” in every circumstance, however dark. Betsie ten Boom gave thanks in Barracks 28. Whatever exactly she said about the fleas, she thanked God in a place designed to break human beings. She did not deny the evil around her, and she did not let it have the last word. Most of us will never be tested as she was. But we can practise, in our smaller trials, the discipline of looking for God’s hand in everything, and giving thanks.

fields.title: The Bottle That Did Not Fail
fields.body_html:
“The jar of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of Jehovah, which he spake by Elijah.”

— 1 Kings 17:16, ASV

A Small Brown Bottle

New arrivals at Ravensbrück had to give up their medicines, but Corrie was allowed to keep a small bottle of liquid vitamins, about half full, as a toilet article. In a camp where women were slowly starving, that was precious. She began giving a few drops each day to the women around her, and before long to many of them. By her account the bottle went on yielding drops for weeks, far longer than it should have, until the women took to calling it the widow’s cruse, after the jar of oil that did not fail in the days of Elijah. When a friend in the camp hospital secretly brought her a supply of vitamins to share, the bottle, she wrote, finally ran dry.

A Story Told in 1945

This is one of the most famous stories in Corrie’s life, and it is worth noting where it comes from. It is not a late addition to her testimony. It appears in full in her 1945 book, written within months of her release, under the heading “The Miracle of the Vitamins.” The essentials there are the same as in the later telling.

No one can now test the story. There is no independent witness, and readers will judge it according to what they believe about God’s dealings with his people. It is possible to imagine natural explanations. Perhaps each dose was smaller than Corrie realised, or the bottle held more than it seemed to. Corrie herself was not naive about such things. She simply told what happened, as she remembered it within a few months, and gave God the glory. Her readers have been free to do the same, or not.

What can be said is that she did not invent it later for effect. And whatever one concludes about the bottle, the more important miracle in the story is not in dispute. In Ravensbrück, where experienced prisoners warned newcomers that the way to survive was to look after oneself alone, a middle-aged Dutch woman spent her precious vitamins on thirty strangers every day.

The Widow’s Cruse

The story the women remembered is in the first book of Kings. During a famine, the prophet Elijah was sent to a widow in the town of Zarephath, outside Israel, who was gathering sticks to bake a last meal for herself and her son before they died. Elijah asked her to make him a small cake first, and promised that her flour and oil would not run out until the famine ended. She did as he asked. “The jar of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of Jehovah, which he spake by Elijah” (1 Kings 17:16, ASV).

The point of the story is not only that God can multiply food. It is that the widow gave first, out of her poverty, and found that God was faithful. Jesus later pointed to her as an example of God’s care for outsiders (Luke 4:25-26). Corrie’s bottle belongs in that line. She gave the little she had, again and again, and found that there was enough.

The Ravensbrück That Destroys

Corrie was sharply aware of the camp’s moral danger. When the Dutch newcomers arrived, prisoners who had been there longer told them that the way to survive was to look after themselves alone. Corrie called that, borrowing a phrase from the Swedish novelist Selma Lagerlöf, “the Ravensbrück that destroys.”

She came to see selfishness as more insidious than cruelty. Cruelty was obvious; selfishness could pass for common sense. Hunger, she observed, can teach a person to pray, and it can also make her think only of herself. She did not exempt herself. She confessed that once, watching a small birthday feast for a dying girl, she caught herself praying that she would be offered some, and was ashamed.

The Ravensbrück That Revives

But Corrie also saw the opposite. There was selfishness in Ravensbrück, she wrote, but there was also love and self-sacrifice. That was the Ravensbrück that revived.

There was the friend from the hospital, whom Corrie never names in her book. She worked late into the night, fed the hungry and clothed the cold, washed patients no one else would touch, and kissed a dirty gypsy child whom everyone else avoided. There was an old woman who got up in the night to carry two heavy stools out to the roll-call ground, so that Betsie, too sick to stand, could sit. When Corrie asked whether they were not too heavy for her, she said that it was the only thing she could still do for others. There was a Dutch nurse who made charcoal from wood to treat the dysentery that was killing so many. And there was a midwife among the prisoners who brought babies into the world in that hell with the same care and joy she would have brought to any nursery.

“Therefore I Could Not Hate”

One more passage from the 1945 book foreshadows the rest of Corrie’s life. A Russian prisoner asked her why the Dutch women seemed so calm and controlled and yet so full of hatred. The question startled her, and she searched her own heart. She saw the cruelty of the regime as clearly as anyone, she wrote, and suffered from it daily. But behind it she saw her Saviour, with his arms open, and so hatred found no place in her. That was written in 1945. She would be tested on it, harder than she could imagine, in the years to come.

For Reflection

The story of the vitamin bottle is usually told as a story about a miracle, and perhaps it was one. But set in its context, it is also a story about a choice. In a place where survival seemed to depend on looking after oneself, Corrie chose to give away what she had. Whether God multiplied the drops or simply honoured the giving, the camp was a little less deadly because of it.

We live in a world that also tells us to look after ourselves first. The widow of Zarephath, the Dutch prisoner with her little bottle, and the old woman carrying stools through the dark all point another way. Give first, even out of poverty, and trust God for what comes after.

fields.title: Betsie
fields.body_html:
“If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, thou art there.”

— Psalm 139:8, ASV

The Elder Sister

Elisabeth ten Boom, always called Betsie, was born on 19 August 1885, nearly seven years before Corrie. She was the eldest of the family. She was never strong. In Corrie’s later books she suffered all her life from anaemia, and she was often the one who stayed at home while others went out. She never married. For most of her adult life she kept house in the Beje, first for her parents and aunts and then for her father and younger sister. She kept the shop’s books, cooked, arranged flowers, welcomed guests, and made the crowded, shabby old house beautiful on very little money.

By every account she was gentle, orderly, and humorous, with a deep and quiet faith. Corrie, lively, impatient, and practical, admired her all her life, and sometimes felt rebuked by her. In the underground years Betsie ran the household of refugees, found beds for everyone, and fed them on ration cards. In prison and camp she became, in Corrie’s telling, the stronger of the two. That was not because she was physically stronger, since she was far weaker. It was because her faith seemed to rest on something that the camp could not reach.

“A Hedge About Her”

Corrie noticed again and again that horrors that overwhelmed her seemed not to touch Betsie. On the day of the executions at Vught, when Corrie laid her head on her sister’s shoulder in despair, Betsie’s face was serene, almost happy. When a frail Dutch woman was beaten to death in Barracks 28, Corrie turned to Betsie in horror and found her face peaceful, her eyes far away, apparently unaware of what had happened. Corrie thought of Satan’s complaint to God about Job: “Hast not thou made a hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath, on every side?” (Job 1:10, ASV). There was a hedge around Betsie too.

It would be wrong to read this as indifference. Betsie was the one who organised the society against grumbling at Vught. She took the hand of a lonely Polish woman and said the name of Jesus to her, and she pitied the officer who beat her during the raid. Once she even went to invite a brutal barracks supervisor to the Bible reading. Her compassion was intense. But the camp’s evil did not seem to get inside her. Near the end, Corrie heard her say something that startled her: she was beginning to love the crowd. Corrie wondered whether her sister was ripening for heaven.

And there is one small line in Corrie’s 1945 book that turns the famous title of her later story around. Betsie depended on her, Corrie wrote, almost like a child, and did not like her to stay away too long. It was, Corrie wrote, as though she were Betsie’s hiding-place in that evil place. The sisters sheltered each other. Corrie gave Betsie practical care and protection. Betsie gave Corrie a faith that kept her from despair.

Plans

In the evenings in Barracks 28 the sisters made plans, and Corrie’s 1945 book records them. When they got home, they would open their house to women coming out of the camps with nowhere to go. If it proved too small, they would find a larger one. They would build a place in Haarlem for young people whose youth had been stolen by the war. And the two of them would go to America and tell what God had done for them.

In the 1971 book these plans became something more: three visions that Betsie saw before her death, of a house in Holland, a former camp in Germany, and a release before the new year. The earlier account gives them as the sisters’ shared hopes, dreamed together in the dark. Either way, a surprising amount of what they planned came true. But Betsie would not be there to see it.

Betsie’s Illness

In the late autumn of 1944 Betsie became seriously ill. Her hands and forehead were burning with fever, but she remained, Corrie wrote, as cheerful and courageous as ever. The sisters went together to the sick roll-call, where hundreds of sick women waited for hours in the cold to be seen, and many died of the waiting. A Dutch nurse brought Betsie to the front of the line, and with a temperature over forty degrees Celsius she was admitted to the hospital barracks. Betsie thanked God for how quickly she had been let in.

The next day Corrie climbed through a washroom window to visit her, and found her sharing a narrow cot with a French girl who kicked her until she fell out of bed. Betsie did not complain. There was such darkness in the heart of the poor French child, she said. It was no accident that she had been put beside her. A nurse caught Corrie and threatened to report her if she came again.

Walking back through the fog, Corrie felt rebellion rise in her. Why did God leave them there so long? Why must Betsie suffer? Why could she not even visit her? Then, she wrote, she heard three words, in French: rempli de tendresse, “filled with tenderness.” There was no one near her. She believed it was God speaking, not in rebuke of her rebellion but in love. She was ashamed and comforted at once.

“Remember Now, Both of Us”

Betsie grew weaker, until she could no longer stand at roll-call and then could not walk at all. The order was that even the dying must appear, and Corrie and a friend carried her out and held her up. Betsie would not hear of dying. She spoke of heaven easily and without fear, but she was sure the two of them would go home together and still do much for others.

In the end a barracks supervisor the sisters had once invited to their Bible reading arranged a stretcher to take Betsie to the hospital. As she was carried away, a Polish prisoner knelt beside her and prayed, a farewell, Corrie felt, from the women to whom Betsie had meant so much. That afternoon Corrie visited her once more. As she was sent away, Betsie called after her: “Remember now, both of us.”

16 December 1944

The next morning Corrie went to the hospital barracks and looked in at the window beside her sister’s bed. Nurses were carrying out a body, wasted almost beyond recognition. It was Betsie.

The date was 16 December 1944. Betsie was fifty-nine. Her death is recorded on the memorial plaque at the family home in Haarlem, and by the Dutch war-graves foundation.

Corrie’s first feeling was desolation. Then, to her own surprise, peace came, and something like joy. The words of Job came to her: “Jehovah gave, and Jehovah hath taken away; blessed be the name of Jehovah” (Job 1:21, ASV). When she went to see her sister’s body among the dead in the washroom, she found that the face looked peaceful and young again, and she took it as a glimpse of heaven in the middle of that place.

“No Pit So Deep”

The words most closely linked with Betsie ten Boom are from The Hiding Place. There Corrie recalls her sister saying, near the end, that they must tell people that there is no pit so deep that God’s love is not deeper still. It is a beautiful saying, and it has comforted countless people. It is always attributed to Betsie, as Corrie attributed it.

The 1945 book does not contain those exact words. It contains a related thought, and it is in Corrie’s own mouth. Speaking at a memorial for women who had died in the barracks, she told her fellow prisoners that for those who belong to the Saviour, death is not a pit into which they fall. It is a tunnel through which they pass into the glorious light of heaven. The two sayings belong together. Betsie may well have said the words the later book gives her, and Corrie may have remembered them clearly. Or the sisters’ shared faith may have found its sharpest expression over years of retelling. What is certain is that the faith behind both sayings was tested in Ravensbrück, and held.

The verse at the head of this chapter says the same thing in the psalmist’s words. “If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, thou art there” (Psalm 139:8, ASV). Sheol is the Old Testament’s name for the grave, the deepest pit there is. Even there, the psalmist says, God is present. There is no place so deep that he is not already there.

A New Sister

That day Corrie spoke at a memorial service in the barracks, on the great resurrection chapter, 1 Corinthians 15. The women had loved Betsie, and the grief was deep.

That night a Russian woman who had nowhere to sleep was being turned away from bunk after bunk. Corrie made room for her in the place beside her where Betsie had lain. They had no language in common, but when Corrie spoke the name of Jesus the woman embraced her. Corrie took it as a sign that God would give her others to love in place of the sister she had lost.

For Reflection

Betsie ten Boom did not survive Ravensbrück. She did not live to see the house in Holland or the home in Germany, or to travel to America. She died as a nameless number in a camp hospital, and her body was carried out in a sheet.

And yet she is remembered, by millions, as one of the great witnesses of the Second World War. That is not because of anything she accomplished. It is because of what she believed and how she believed it: gratefully, gently, and without fear, in the worst place on earth. Her sister carried her message out into the world for another forty years. It was the message of the psalm: even if we make our bed in Sheol, God is there.
