It contains a related thought, and it is in Corrie’s own mouth. Speaking at a memorial for women who had died in the barracks, she told her fellow prisoners that for those who belong to the Saviour, death is not a pit into which they fall. It is a tunnel through which they pass into the glorious light of heaven. The two sayings belong together. Betsie may well have said the words the later book gives her, and Corrie may have remembered them clearly. Or the sisters’ shared faith may have found its sharpest expression over years of retelling. What is certain is that the faith behind both sayings was tested in Ravensbrück, and held. The verse at the head of this chapter says the same thing in the psalmist’s words. “If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, thou art there” (Psalm 139:8, ASV). Sheol is the Old Testament’s name for the grave, the deepest pit there is. Even there, the psalmist says, God is present. There is no place so deep that he is not already there. A New Sister That day Corrie spoke at a memorial service in the barracks, on the great resurrection chapter, 1 Corinthians 15. The women had loved Betsie, and the grief was deep. That night a Russian woman who had nowhere to sleep was being turned away from bunk after bunk. Corrie made room for her in the place beside her where Betsie had lain. They had no language in common, but when Corrie spoke the name of Jesus the woman embraced her. Corrie took it as a sign that God would give her others to love in place of the sister she had lost. For Reflection Betsie ten Boom did not survive Ravensbrück. She did not live to see the house in Holland or the home in Germany, or to travel to America. She died as a nameless number in a camp hospital, and her body was carried out in a sheet. And yet she is remembered, by millions, as one of the great witnesses of the Second World War. That is not because of anything she accomplished. It is because of what she believed and how she believed it: gratefully, gently, and without fear, in the worst place on earth. Her sister carried her message out into the world for another forty years. It was the message of the psalm: even if we make our bed in Sheol, God is there.

fields.title: Entlassen
fields.body_html:
“Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: The snare is broken, and we are escaped.”

— Psalm 124:7, ASV

Punishment for a Dead Woman

The day after Betsie died, a Sunday, the whole of Barracks 28 was punished with a disciplinary roll-call. One of the fourteen hundred women had failed to appear. The prisoners stood in the cold from half past five in the morning until noon while they were counted and recounted. At last the missing woman was found. She was a Polish prisoner, lying dead in her bunk. The whole barracks had been punished for the absence of a dead woman.

Five women, Corrie among them, became ill after that roll-call, with swollen legs and a wasting that grew worse day by day. Within ten days, Corrie wrote, the other four were dead.

“Ten Boom, Cornelia”

Three days after Betsie’s death, Corrie’s name was called at morning roll-call. She went forward expecting some new danger, and found instead that she was being discharged. Other prisoners told her how lucky she was. But first a doctor found her legs swollen with oedema, and since released prisoners had to leave the camp apparently healthy, she was sent to the hospital barracks until the swelling went down.

A Week in the Hospital Barracks

That week, Corrie wrote, was among the worst of her imprisonment. She lay among the gravely sick and wounded while she waited for clearance, and some of her fellow released prisoners were cruel to those around them. At night the sickest could not reach the icy latrine, and some did not survive trying. Corrie took on the work of helping them, and talked to them about Jesus as she did.

In one bed lay a young girl with a learning disability, desperately ill, crying for her mother. Her name was Oelie. Night by night Corrie spoke to her of the Saviour, and on the last night the girl was able to tell her, simply and in her own words, that Jesus loved her, had borne her punishment, and was preparing a place for her. They gave thanks together. Corrie wrote that she understood then why she had been kept that week. Her classes for disabled people in Haarlem had come to this.

Eight Hours

One night that week Corrie walked down the hospital corridor and saw that the windows were thick with frost and the water in the bucket was frozen solid. It was the first night of the bitter winter cold. She no longer had to stand at roll-call. In the morning she lay in her bunk and heard the rhythmic stamping of thousands of feet outside, as the prisoners stood for an hour and a half in the icy wind.

Weeks before, as she and Betsie walked to night roll-call, she had felt God promise her that she would be free before the severe cold came. She had told the other women at the Bible reading that they would all be freed before the cold. She had been wrong, she wrote. The promise was for her alone. God, she wrote, had saved her eight hours before the onset of severe cold.

The Gate

At last she was cleared. She was given clothes, a bundle of her own and Betsie’s belongings, and a discharge certificate, reproduced in her 1945 book, bearing her prisoner number, 66730. The date of her release is given in Dutch sources as 28 December 1944.

At the gate she learned that more of the Dutch women had died, among them one who had at first mocked the Bible readings and had later, by Betsie’s account, come to faith. Corrie walked out comforted, believing that even Betsie’s death had not been without fruit. Walking to the station through the snow, past women still being driven to their work, she felt how much grief she was leaving behind.

Home Through Germany

The journey home through a collapsing Germany took several days, with a sick young Dutch woman named Claire Prins as her companion. They had almost no food and no ration coupons. Corrie met both cruelty and kindness on the way: a welfare office that shut the door on her, a Red Cross nurse who fed her secretly, a soldier who treated her with contempt, and one family who gave the two women a meal and, for a few minutes, a glimpse of the decent Germany she had known before the war. At the border, at Nieuweschans, strangers helped the two exhausted women onto a Dutch train, and Corrie felt that at last she could begin to enjoy her freedom.

Groningen

In Groningen she went to a deaconess hospital. One of the nurses turned out to have been a leader in her own girls’ clubs, and did not at first recognise the gaunt woman in front of her. They fed her, bathed her, and found her clean clothes, and she slept in a real bed. When she heard music again for the first time, she wept. Her life, she wrote, had been given back to her as a gift.

Why Was She Released?

For the rest of her life, Corrie told audiences that she had been released through a clerical error. In The Hiding Place she says that she learned this much later. She also says that about a week after her release, all the women of her age group in the camp were sent to the gas chamber. The museum in Haarlem records that she learned of the “error” on a return visit to Ravensbrück, around 1959.

It is worth saying carefully what can and cannot be known. No document has been found showing that her release was a mistake. Her 1945 book, written within months, never calls it one. That book shows, as we have seen, that in 1944 the sisters expected their prison term to end at a fixed date. At Vught they wrote home asking whether it would end in September or December. Corrie was released alongside several other women who were also being discharged, some of whom had waited two months for medical clearance. That pattern fits an ordinary, if much delayed, release at the end of a sentence, at least as well as it fits a mistake. As for the gas chamber, the historical record shows that Ravensbrück’s gas chamber began operating in late January 1945. That was about a month after Corrie’s release, not a week. Selections of the sick, the weak, and older women for killing did take place in the last months of 1944 and early 1945, by transports and other means. Corrie herself had seen one of the transports leave.

So the honest conclusion is this. Corrie was discharged, for reasons never fully explained. Years later she was told it had been a clerical mistake, and she believed it. Whatever the cause, the danger she escaped was real. A sick woman of fifty-two with swollen legs had every reason to fear the weeks that followed at Ravensbrück, and within weeks the camp began gassing the sick and the old. Her conviction that God had brought her out of the snare does not depend on whether the paperwork was a mistake.

The psalm at the head of this chapter is a song of thanksgiving for exactly that kind of escape. “If it had not been Jehovah who was on our side … Then they had swallowed us up alive” (Psalm 124:2-3, ASV). And then: “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: The snare is broken, and we are escaped” (Psalm 124:7, ASV). The bird does not know how the snare came to break. It only knows that it is free.

For Reflection

Corrie came home to Haarlem in January 1945, alone, and walked into the Beje, still occupied Holland, with her father and sister gone. Watches left for repair, rugs, and books had been stolen. But her piano was still there, and her father’s portrait and his chair. She stood by her father’s bed and thought of him and Betsie seeing the answers to all their questions, and she dared to be happy.

She had been given her life back. What she would do with it is the subject of the rest of this book.

fields.title: A Letter to the Informer
fields.body_html:
“but I say unto you, Love your enemies, and pray for them that persecute you”

— Matthew 5:44, ASV

Liberation

Corrie came home to an occupied country in its hardest winter. The winter of 1944 and 1945 is remembered in the Netherlands as the Hunger Winter. In the western provinces, still under German control, food and fuel ran out, and some twenty thousand people died of hunger and cold. In Haarlem the people cut down the trees in the parks for firewood. Corrie’s 1945 book mentions a great wild cherry in the Kenaupark, known as the bride of Haarlem, whose blossoms she and Betsie and their father had gone to see every spring. It was chopped down for fuel that winter. When she went to look for it, it was gone.

On 5 May 1945 the German forces in the Netherlands surrendered. Corrie described the first service in the liberated Grote Kerk, with the minute of silence for the dead and the national anthem that she could not bring herself to sing. She named them in her heart: her father, Betsie, someone she calls Piet, and so many others. She described the crowds, the orange flags, and the singing in the streets outside her window.

Shaved Heads

She also described something else, and it tells us a great deal about her. In the first days of freedom, crowds in Haarlem, as all over the liberated Netherlands, seized women accused of relationships with German soldiers, shaved their heads in public, and mocked them.

Corrie watched from the edge of the crowd, and she did not join in. One of the girls reminded her of the young women she had known in the camp, and she felt pity, not triumph. She understood why people wanted revenge after five years of humiliation. But she was sure this was not the right way, and she went home. She thanked God that the day of reckoning so many had feared had not been bloodier, and wondered whether prayer had restrained it.

A woman just out of Ravensbrück, whose father and sister had died at German hands, stood in the town square and pitied the women whose heads were being shaved. That pity was already the beginning of her life’s second work.

The Cost Counted

The war had cost the ten Boom family dearly. Casper had died in prison in March 1944 and Betsie in Ravensbrück in December. Willem’s son Kik, arrested separately in the summer of 1944 for resistance work, had been taken through a series of camps to Bergen-Belsen. The Dutch war-graves foundation gives his death there in the spring of 1945. Willem himself had been released soon after the raid, but he had caught an illness in prison, usually described as spinal tuberculosis. He died on 13 December 1946. Nollie survived, and lived until 1953.

The Beje had been emptied and plundered. The watches left for repair had been stolen, along with rugs and books. By her later account, she tried to take up the watch shop again, but her heart was no longer in it. She found herself restless, and she knew why. She was supposed to be telling people what she and Betsie had learned.

A Book in June

By June 1945, just weeks after liberation, her first book was in print in Amsterdam. It was the short, vivid account of prison and camp that this biography has drawn on throughout. It closes with a postlude that looks forward to a home for people coming back from the camps, in the spirit of Betsie’s plans. It was the beginning of her public witness.

A Letter

On 19 June 1945, Corrie wrote a letter to the man who, as she understood it, had betrayed her family to the Gestapo. The letter was published thirty years later, in 1975, in a collection of her prison letters. As published, it tells him that she had heard he was most probably the one who had betrayed them. She wrote that her father had died because of it, and her sister in the camp. She said that she had suffered too, and that she forgave him everything. She told him that she was praying for him, and that she was sending him a New Testament, because Jesus had borne his sins and could make him new.

This book has already noted how uncertain the informer’s identity and fate are. The later books name him as Jan Vogel. A Dutch local historian gives the name as H. van Vogel. The museum says that he was sentenced to death, came to faith shortly before his execution, and was executed. But no one of that name appears on the list of people executed under Dutch postwar justice, and many death sentences were commuted. The court records that could settle the question are not public. So we do not know what became of the man, whether the letter reached him, or how he answered. The story of his conversion before execution may be true, or it may have drifted into his story from someone else’s. What we have is the letter, and the date on it.

The date matters. In June 1945 the Netherlands was only a few weeks free. The hunger, grief, and anger were raw everywhere. The special courts for collaborators had barely begun their work. Corrie did not wait until the pain had faded, or until justice had been done, or until the man had asked for forgiveness. She wrote barely six months after Betsie’s death, and about five months after her own return from Ravensbrück.

“Love Your Enemies”

The command at the head of this chapter is perhaps the hardest thing Jesus ever said. “But I say unto you, Love your enemies, and pray for them that persecute you” (Matthew 5:44, ASV). He gave a reason: “that ye may be sons of your Father who is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and the good” (Matthew 5:45, ASV). We are to love our enemies because God loves his, and we were once among them. “While we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10, ASV).

It is important to be clear about what Corrie’s letter did and did not do. It did not deny that the man had done wrong. It named what he had done, and what it had cost. Nor did it ask the Dutch courts to let him go. Forgiveness in Scripture is not the same as pretending no harm was done, or as abolishing justice. Paul, in the same passage where he tells the Romans never to avenge themselves, reminds them that vengeance belongs to God. The next chapter speaks of rulers who bear the sword (Romans 12:19; 13:4). What Corrie did was give up her own claim to repayment. She handed the debt to God, and wished the man well, which meant wishing that he would come to know Christ. “And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving each other, even as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32, ASV).

She would struggle with forgiveness for the rest of her life, and she said so openly. The 1945 letter was not the end of the struggle. It was a decision made at the beginning, before she could have felt much of the forgiveness she wrote about. Later she liked to say that forgiveness is an act of the will, and that the feelings follow. The letter to the informer is the earliest evidence we have that she believed this, and acted on it.

For Reflection

In the first weeks after liberation, Corrie ten Boom did two things that most of her neighbours did not. She pitied the women whose heads were being shaved in the square, and she wrote to the man who had betrayed her family to tell him she forgave him.

Neither act undid the past or brought back her father or sister. But both were signs of a heart that had been changed in Ravensbrück, a heart that could not hate, as she had written in the camp. Most of us are called to forgive smaller wrongs than hers. Her example suggests that we should not wait until we feel like it. We can decide, and write the letter, and trust God to bring the feelings after.

fields.title: Homes for the Broken
fields.body_html:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”

— Romans 12:21, ASV

A House in the Woods

Corrie’s 1945 book closes with a postlude that she clearly saw as an answer to prayer. She is shown a fine house in the woods near Haarlem that is to become a home for people coming back from the camps, and she remembers Betsie describing such a house in Ravensbrück, down to the beauty of its woodwork. She hoped it would be a place of real recovery, not merely of rest.

The house became a reality. According to the museum and the Dutch women’s biographical lexicon, Corrie opened a home for people recovering from the war in Bloemendaal, a wooded village just outside Haarlem, first in a villa called Schapenduinen and later in another house, Zonneduinen, bought by a foundation set up to support the work. In 1945 she already hoped that it might later serve others who needed healing too.

In The Hiding Place Corrie adds that among the people who came to the house were Dutch men and women who had collaborated with the Germans. After liberation, many of them were despised and rejected by their neighbours. She tells of former prisoners and former collaborators learning to live under the same roof. That detail comes only from the later book, but it fits entirely with what we saw in the town square in May 1945.

Plans Made in the Dark

It is striking how many of the plans the two sisters made in Barracks 28 came true. Corrie opened a home in the Netherlands for those coming out of the camps. She travelled to America and told the story of God’s faithfulness. The grand clubhouse in the centre of Haarlem seems not to have come about in the form they imagined, and Betsie was not there to see any of it.

There is a lesson here that Corrie often drew. Betsie’s faith had looked unrealistic in the camp. She had been sure they would both go home, and she was wrong about that. But she was right about far more than she was wrong about. The plans she made while dying in a lice-ridden bunk were not fantasies. They were, in their way, prophecies. God did not give her what she expected. He gave the work she had seen to her sister to carry out.

A Camp in Germany

In 1949 the work extended in a direction Corrie could hardly have planned in 1945. With the help of the Protestant church in Germany, she opened a home in Darmstadt, in the west of Germany. It was in a former camp, and it took in refugees and displaced people. Germany after the war was full of them: millions of Germans expelled from the east, bombed-out families, and people with nowhere to go. Some popular accounts say it was a former concentration camp. The sources are not clear about exactly what kind of camp it had been, and this book will not claim more than they do. The Darmstadt home ran until 1960.

In the later framing of The Hiding Place, this was the second of Betsie’s “visions.” Betsie had seen a camp in Germany, once used for cruelty, that would be painted bright colours and used for healing. Whatever words Betsie actually used in Ravensbrück, the fact is remarkable. Within five years of walking out of a German concentration camp, Corrie ten Boom was running a home for Germans.

Preaching to the Guards

Corrie’s 1953 book Amazing Love includes a story from these years that is less famous than the encounter in Munich, and in some ways more striking. After the war, the Allies held many former camp personnel in internment camps while they awaited trial or release. Among them were women who had served as guards at Ravensbrück. Corrie went to preach to them.

She tells of speaking in such a camp to a group of former women guards, the Aufseherinnen she had feared and despised. At first they received her coldly. She spoke to them, as she spoke to everyone, of the love of Christ that had reached her in the camp and could reach them too. She called the chapter “My Chocolate Sermon.” Readers who want the details should read it in her own words. What matters here is that she tells of it, and that she wrote about it in 1953, long before the more famous story of Munich reached print.

“Overcome Evil with Good”

The verse at the head of this chapter concludes Paul’s great passage about how Christians should treat those who harm them. “Render to no man evil for evil,” he writes. “Avenge not yourselves, beloved, but give place unto the wrath of God.” Then: “But if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him to drink.” And finally: “Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:17, 19, 20, 21, ASV).

Corrie’s postwar work is a practical commentary on those verses. A German camp had been a place of evil. She took a German camp and made it a place of healing. German guards had been the instruments of her suffering. She went to preach the gospel to German guards. Dutch collaborators had betrayed people like her family to the Gestapo, and according to her later account she took collaborators into her home. None of this denied that evil had been done. It simply refused to let evil have the last word, or to answer it in kind.

It should also be said that this was not easy for her, or quick. In her later books Corrie was frank about her struggles. She could preach forgiveness in public while nursing bitterness in private against people who had wronged her in small ways. She said that she had to learn forgiveness again and again. Overcoming evil with good was not a single victory but a long campaign.

For Reflection

It would have been entirely understandable if Corrie ten Boom had spent the rest of her life avoiding anything German. Instead, within five years of her release, she was running a home in Germany, preaching to former camp guards, and sheltering people her own neighbours despised.

Most of us have someone, or some group of people, whose wrongs against us or against those we love make us want to keep our distance for ever. Paul’s command does not require us to pretend the wrong did not happen. It invites us to do the harder, braver thing: to answer evil with good, and so refuse to let it define us.

fields.title: The Hand in Munich
fields.body_html:
“and hope putteth not to shame; because the love of God hath been shed abroad in our hearts through the Holy Spirit which was given unto us.”

— Romans 5:5, ASV

The Most Famous Handshake

Of all the stories Corrie ten Boom told, none has been retold more often than this one. It is also, like several of the best-known scenes in her life, a story that rests entirely on her own later account, so it deserves to be told carefully and briefly. Readers who want it in her own words will find it in The Hiding Place and Tramp for the Lord.

As she told it, the year was 1947 and the place a church in Munich, where she had just spoken about God’s forgiveness. As the audience left, a man came forward whom she recognised as one of the guards at Ravensbrück. It was a man from the place where new prisoners had been processed and humiliated. He did not recognise her. He told her that he had since become a Christian and believed God had forgiven him, but he wanted to hear forgiveness from one of the women who had suffered there. He held out his hand.

Corrie found, to her dismay, that she could not take it. She, who had been preaching forgiveness all over Europe, felt nothing but the memory of Betsie and that room. So she prayed silently, telling Jesus that she could not forgive this man and asking him to supply what she lacked. Then, as an act of obedience rather than feeling, she put out her hand. As their hands met, she said, she felt a warmth of love flow through her that she knew was not her own, and she was able to tell him from her heart that she forgave him.

The lesson she drew from it was that forgiveness is not something we manufacture. God, who commands us to love our enemies, also gives the love we need to obey.

What We Can Know

It is important to say what kind of evidence this story is. It is Corrie’s own account, and there is no other. The man is never named. No one else who was present has ever come forward, and no record of the meeting exists apart from her telling of it. The story first appears in print about twenty-five years after the event: at the end of The Hiding Place in 1971, and in a magazine article the following year. It appears again in Tramp for the Lord in 1974. By then Corrie had told it many times from the platform, and the versions differ in small details, as spoken stories do.

Her 1953 book Amazing Love, written much closer to the time, does not tell this story. It tells the different story, described in the last chapter, of preaching to former women guards in an internment camp. That does not mean the Munich encounter did not happen. Corrie may simply not have written about it for many years, or may have found it too personal. But it does mean that the famous version, with its vivid details of the grey overcoat and the current of warmth, reaches us as a memory shaped by many retellings.

None of this makes the story less true in the sense that matters most. Corrie told it as her own experience, again and again, to people who knew her. And the central claim of the story fits everything else we know of her life. She could not forgive by her own strength. When she obeyed anyway, God supplied the love. That is exactly what she had written in Ravensbrück, when she said that her Saviour’s love filled her heart so that she could not hate. It is exactly what she had done in June 1945, when she wrote to the informer before she could have felt much forgiveness at all. The Munich story is the most dramatic version of a pattern that runs through her whole life.

“The Love of God Shed Abroad”

The museum that now occupies the Beje connects this story with the verse at the head of this chapter, and it is well chosen. “Hope putteth not to shame; because the love of God hath been shed abroad in our hearts through the Holy Spirit which was given unto us” (Romans 5:5, ASV).

Paul’s point is that the love of God is not only something we learn about. It is something poured into us. The Holy Spirit fills us with a love we could not produce. In the next few verses Paul explains what kind of love this is: “But God commendeth his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8, ASV). It is love for enemies. What Corrie felt in Munich was, in her understanding, exactly this love. It was God’s love for the guard, passing through her because she could not supply it herself.

Forgiveness as Obedience

Corrie drew practical lessons from the story, and she taught them wherever she went. Forgiveness, she said, is an act of the will, and the will can act whatever the heart happens to feel. We do not wait until we feel forgiving. We obey, and trust God to change our feelings.

This is a teaching with deep roots in Scripture. When Peter asked how often he must forgive a brother, as many as seven times, Jesus answered, “until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22, ASV). He then told the parable of a servant who had been forgiven a vast debt and then refused to forgive a fellow servant a small one. The parable ends with a warning: “So shall also my heavenly Father do unto you, if ye forgive not every one his brother from your hearts” (Matthew 18:35, ASV). Forgiveness is not optional for those who have been forgiven. But neither is it something we must manufacture alone. The same Lord who commands it gives it.

Corrie was also honest that forgiveness is not a single event. In later years she told stories against herself about Christian friends who had wronged her in small matters, whom she found much harder to forgive than the Ravensbrück guard. She said that she forgave them, and then found the bitterness coming back, and had to forgive again. That honesty is part of what made her testimony believable. She never claimed to have mastered forgiveness. She claimed only that God had given it to her when she could not give it herself.

For Reflection

The story of the handshake in Munich has helped countless people who were struggling to forgive. It helps precisely because Corrie did not pretend to be a saint. She stood there, a famous preacher of forgiveness, and found that she could not do it. What she did next is open to anyone. She told God the truth about her heart, asked for his love, and obeyed with her hand before her feelings followed.

Whom do we find it impossible to forgive? Corrie’s answer would be simple. Tell God you cannot, ask him for his forgiveness, and hold out your hand. The love of God, she would say, has been shed abroad in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. It is not ours to produce. It is ours to receive, and to pass on.

fields.title: Sixty Countries
fields.body_html:
“preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all longsuffering and teaching.”

— 2 Timothy 4:2, ASV

America, 1946

In 1946, a little more than a year after her release, Corrie ten Boom crossed the Atlantic for the first time. She spent about ten months in the United States and Canada, speaking wherever she was invited, in churches, colleges, prisons, and homes. She had almost no money and no organisation behind her. By her later account she arrived with very little money, and she went from one invitation to the next. It was the fulfilment of one of the plans the sisters had made in Barracks 28, that they would go to America and tell of the marvellous way God had kept them. Corrie went alone.

It was the beginning of more than thirty years of almost constant travel. The museum and the Dutch sources say that she spoke in more than sixty countries. She travelled on several continents, including behind the Iron Curtain in Communist Europe. The archives at Wheaton College in Illinois, which hold her papers, include five passports from the years 1948 to 1971, thick with stamps. She had no settled home for much of that time. She called herself, in the title of a later book, a tramp for the Lord.

“Jesus Is Victor”

Her message was simple, and she repeated it thousands of times. She told her story: the watch shop, the hiding place, the raid, her father’s death, Ravensbrück, and Betsie. But the story was never the point. The point was what she and Betsie had learned there: that God’s love is stronger than the deepest darkness, that Jesus is the conqueror, and that forgiveness is possible because God gives it.

“Jesus is Victor” was her motto all her life. It had hung on the fireplace in the Beje on the day of the raid, burned into a wooden plaque. The phrase echoes the cry associated with the nineteenth-century German pastor Johann Christoph Blumhardt, Jesus ist Sieger, which was widely used among Dutch and German Christians of the holiness tradition. Corrie wrote it in autograph books, repeated it at the end of talks, and returned to it in every crisis. The phrase runs all through her 1945 book in another form: Jesus is the Conqueror.

The Circles She Moved In

Corrie’s theology was shaped first by the Dutch Reformed Church in which she grew up, and by the warm evangelical piety of the Réveil that lay behind her family’s faith. After the war she moved in wider circles. Her early English books were published by the Christian Literature Crusade, the publishing arm of the Worldwide Evangelization Crusade. The foreword to her 1953 book Amazing Love was written by Norman Grubb, a leading teacher of the “victorious Christian life” associated with the Keswick movement. In later decades she worked closely with Youth for Christ, and she became a friend of Billy Graham, whose film company made the movie of her story. She was welcomed in Pentecostal and charismatic circles as well. She appeared, for example, with the healing evangelist Kathryn Kuhlman, and spoke at the Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization in 1974 about the power of the Holy Spirit.

She was, in other words, an evangelical of broad sympathies. She was at home with anyone who loved Jesus, and she was less interested in denominational lines than in whether people knew him. That was already true in Ravensbrück, where she had reflected that there would be no separate Protestant and Catholic areas in heaven.

The Hiding Place

In the late 1960s the American writers John and Elizabeth Sherrill met Corrie and heard her story. They spent many hours interviewing her. The result was The Hiding Place, published by Chosen Books in 1971. It became one of the best-selling Christian books of its generation and has been translated into dozens of languages. In 1975 World Wide Pictures, the film company of the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, released a film version, directed by James F. Collier. It was shown in cinemas around the world and brought her story to many who would never have read the book.

This biography has compared The Hiding Place with Corrie’s earlier accounts, and noted that some of its most famous scenes do not appear in them. That comparison is not a criticism of the book. The Hiding Place is a work of great skill and real truthfulness, and it is the book through which most people have met Corrie ten Boom. It is also a book written a quarter of a century after the events, by professional writers shaping her memories for a wide audience. It stands in the same relation to her 1945 account that a mature testimony stands to a diary. Both are true. They are not the same kind of truth.

Honours

Honours came, late. In 1962 Queen Juliana made her a knight of the Order of Orange-Nassau. On 12 December 1967 Yad Vashem, Israel’s memorial to the victims of the Holocaust, recognised her as one of the Righteous Among the Nations, the title given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews. A tree was planted in her honour on the Avenue of the Righteous in Jerusalem. The ceremony took place on 28 February 1968, twenty-four years to the day after the raid on the Beje. The family’s century of prayer for the peace of Jerusalem had come, in a sense, full circle.

She also went back to Ravensbrück. The dates given in the sources differ, around 1959 by the museum’s account, perhaps later by others. The camp was then in Communist East Germany. It was on that visit, according to the museum, that she learned what she came to believe was the clerical error behind her release.

Controversies

Corrie ten Boom was widely loved, but she was not above criticism, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Three matters deserve brief mention.

First, in the strict Reformed circles of her own country, some objected on principle to a woman preaching. Corrie did not defend herself at length. She simply went on speaking where she was invited. Even those who disagreed with her on this point generally spoke of her with respect.

Second, in the 1960s and 1970s she taught about spiritual warfare, demonic oppression, and deliverance, notably in a booklet called Defeated Enemies published in 1962. Her growing association with charismatic circles made some of her admirers uneasy. Christians who do not share that emphasis may find parts of her later teaching unconvincing. But she held it in the same spirit as everything else, as part of her conviction that Jesus is victor over every power.

Third, a letter warning against belief in a secret pre-tribulation rapture of the church has circulated widely under her name. It is said to date from 1974 and to draw on her experience of Christians unprepared for persecution. It is quoted in several books. But its origin has never been verified, and it should not be quoted as hers without the original document.

None of these controversies touches the core of her witness. She never claimed to be a theologian. She was a witness who told what she had seen, and pointed to the One who had kept her.

Better Known Abroad

There is one irony in Corrie’s fame. For much of her life she was far better known in the United States than in her own country. The phrase “unknown in her own land” recurs in Dutch writing about her. For years the museum in Haarlem drew most of its visitors from abroad. Only in recent decades, as the Netherlands has reckoned more fully with its wartime history, have Dutch visitors come in equal numbers.

For Reflection

Paul’s charge to Timothy, at the head of this chapter, was written near the end of his own life: “preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2, ASV). For more than thirty years Corrie ten Boom did just that, in season and out, in comfortable churches and behind the Iron Curtain, before crowds and before single listeners. She was not an eloquent speaker in the usual sense. Her English was accented, her stories were simple, and she repeated herself. But she had seen something, and she could not stop telling it.

Most of us will not travel to sixty countries. But all of us have seen something of God’s faithfulness, in small ways or large. The question her life puts to us is whether we are telling it.

She called herself, in the title of a later book, a tramp for the Lord. “Jesus Is Victor” Her message was simple, and she repeated it thousands of times. She told her story: the watch shop, the hiding place, the raid, her father’s death, Ravensbrück, and Betsie. But the story was never the point. The point was what she and Betsie had learned there: that God’s love is stronger than the deepest darkness, that Jesus is the conqueror, and that forgiveness is possible because God gives it. “Jesus is Victor” was her motto all her life. It had hung on the fireplace in the Beje on the day of the raid, burned into a wooden plaque. The phrase echoes the cry associated with the nineteenth-century German pastor Johann Christoph Blumhardt, Jesus ist Sieger, which was widely used among Dutch and German Christians of the holiness tradition. Corrie wrote it in autograph books, repeated it at the end of talks, and returned to it in every crisis. The phrase runs all through her 1945 book in another form: Jesus is the Conqueror. The Circles She Moved In Corrie’s theology was shaped first by the Dutch Reformed Church in which she grew up, and by the warm evangelical piety of the Réveil that lay behind her family’s faith. After the war she moved in wider circles. Her early English books were published by the Christian Literature Crusade, the publishing arm of the Worldwide Evangelization Crusade. The foreword to her 1953 book Amazing Love was written by Norman Grubb, a leading teacher of the “victorious Christian life” associated with the Keswick movement. In later decades she worked closely with Youth for Christ, and she became a friend of Billy Graham, whose film company made the movie of her story. She was welcomed in Pentecostal and charismatic circles as well. She appeared, for example, with the healing evangelist Kathryn Kuhlman, and spoke at the Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization in 1974 about the power of the Holy Spirit. She was, in other words, an evangelical of broad sympathies. She was at home with anyone who loved Jesus, and she was less interested in denominational lines than in whether people knew him. That was already true in Ravensbrück, where she had reflected that there would be no separate Protestant and Catholic areas in heaven. The Hiding Place In the late 1960s the American writers John and Elizabeth Sherrill met Corrie and heard her story. They spent many hours interviewing her. The result was The Hiding Place, published by Chosen Books in 1971. It became one of the best-selling Christian books of its generation and has been translated into dozens of languages. In 1975 World Wide Pictures, the film company of the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, released a film version, directed by James F. Collier. It was shown in cinemas around the world and brought her story to many who would never have read the book. This biography has compared The Hiding Place with Corrie’s earlier accounts, and noted that some of its most famous scenes do not appear in them. That comparison is not a criticism of the book. The Hiding Place is a work of great skill and real truthfulness, and it is the book through which most people have met Corrie ten Boom. It is also a book written a quarter of a century after the events, by professional writers shaping her memories for a wide audience. It stands in the same relation to her 1945 account that a mature testimony stands to a diary. Both are true. They are not the same kind of truth. Honours Honours came, late. In 1962 Queen Juliana made her a knight of the Order of Orange-Nassau. On 12 December 1967 Yad Vashem, Israel’s memorial to the victims of the Holocaust, recognised her as one of the Righteous Among the Nations, the title given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews. A tree was planted in her honour on the Avenue of the Righteous in Jerusalem. The ceremony took place on 28 February 1968, twenty-four years to the day after the raid on the Beje. The family’s century of prayer for the peace of Jerusalem had come, in a sense, full circle. She also went back to Ravensbrück. The dates given in the sources differ, around 1959 by the museum’s account, perhaps later by others. The camp was then in Communist East Germany. It was on that visit, according to the museum, that she learned what she came to believe was the clerical error behind her release. Controversies Corrie ten Boom was widely loved, but she was not above criticism, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Three matters deserve brief mention. First, in the strict Reformed circles of her own country, some objected on principle to a woman preaching. Corrie did not defend herself at length. She simply went on speaking where she was invited. Even those who disagreed with her on this point generally spoke of her with respect. Second, in the 1960s and 1970s she taught about spiritual warfare, demonic oppression, and deliverance, notably in a booklet called Defeated Enemies published in 1962. Her growing association with charismatic circles made some of her admirers uneasy. Christians who do not share that emphasis may find parts of her later teaching unconvincing. But she held it in the same spirit as everything else, as part of her conviction that Jesus is victor over every power. Third, a letter warning against belief in a secret pre-tribulation rapture of the church has circulated widely under her name. It is said to date from 1974 and to draw on her experience of Christians unprepared for persecution. It is quoted in several books. But its origin has never been verified, and it should not be quoted as hers without the original document. None of these controversies touches the core of her witness. She never claimed to be a theologian. She was a witness who told what she had seen, and pointed to the One who had kept her. Better Known Abroad There is one irony in Corrie’s fame. For much of her life she was far better known in the United States than in her own country. The phrase “unknown in her own land” recurs in Dutch writing about her. For years the museum in Haarlem drew most of its visitors from abroad. Only in recent decades, as the Netherlands has reckoned more fully with its wartime history, have Dutch visitors come in equal numbers. For Reflection Paul’s charge to Timothy, at the head of this chapter, was written near the end of his own life: “preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2, ASV). For more than thirty years Corrie ten Boom did just that, in season and out, in comfortable churches and behind the Iron Curtain, before crowds and before single listeners. She was not an eloquent speaker in the usual sense. Her English was accented, her stories were simple, and she repeated herself. But she had seen something, and she could not stop telling it. Most of us will not travel to sixty countries. But all of us have seen something of God’s faithfulness, in small ways or large. The question her life puts to us is whether we are telling it.

fields.title: The Five Silent Years
fields.body_html:
“and even to old age I am he, and even to hoar hairs will I carry you; I have made, and I will bear; yea, I will carry, and will deliver.”

— Isaiah 46:4, ASV

A Home at Last

For most of the three decades after the war Corrie ten Boom had no settled home. She lived out of suitcases, stayed with friends, and moved from one invitation to the next. She was accompanied on her travels by a series of younger women who acted as companions and secretaries. In her eighties the travelling finally became too much. In 1977, according to the museum, she settled permanently in the United States, in a house in Placentia, in Orange County, California.

She was eighty-five. She hoped to go on working from there, and for about a year she did.

Strokes

On 23 August 1978 Corrie suffered a stroke that took away most of her power of speech. More strokes followed. After a severe one in October 1980 she was confined to bed and could no longer walk. For the last five years of her life, the woman who had spoken to audiences in more than sixty countries could say almost nothing.

She was cared for through those years by two women in particular. Pamela Rosewell, an Englishwoman who had been Corrie’s travelling companion, stayed on to nurse her, together with Lotte Reimeringer. Pamela Rosewell, later Pamela Rosewell Moore, afterwards wrote a book about this period called The Five Silent Years of Corrie ten Boom. Anyone who wants to know about Corrie’s last years should read it. It tells of a woman who could no longer preach, but who still communicated with her eyes, her hands, and a few sounds. She still welcomed visitors, still prayed, and still, in some way her carers found hard to describe, ministered to those around her.

Her Mother’s Silence

It is hard not to notice the echo. Sixty years earlier, Corrie had watched her own mother decline through a series of strokes until she could say only a few words. Corrie remembered all her life how her mother’s love had gone on expressing itself through the little she could still do. Now Corrie herself lay in a room, nearly silent, depending on others for everything, and loving them through the little she could still do.

There is something fitting about it, though it cannot have felt fitting to her. The woman whose life had been defined by what she said, her testimony, her stories, and her preaching, spent her last years unable to say it. Her witness in those years was simply her presence, and the patience with which she accepted what she could not change. She had learned in solitary confinement at Scheveningen that God could be very near in silence and helplessness. She learned it again in Placentia.

“Even to Old Age”

The verse at the head of this chapter is one of the tenderest promises in the prophets. Isaiah contrasts the idols of Babylon, which have to be carried by their worshippers on the backs of weary animals, with the living God, who carries his people. “Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob … that have been borne by me from their birth, that have been carried from the womb; and even to old age I am he, and even to hoar hairs will I carry you” (Isaiah 46:3-4, ASV).

Corrie’s life had begun, by family tradition, with a premature birth so frail that no one expected her to live. It ended in the helplessness of old age. At both ends she was carried. In between, she had carried a great deal: refugees, ration cards, the burden of the underground, her dying sister, and the message she had been given in Ravensbrück. At the end, she was carried again. God, as Isaiah says, had made her, and he would bear her, carry her, and deliver her.

15 April 1983

Corrie ten Boom died at home in Placentia late in the evening of 15 April 1983. It was her ninety-first birthday. A memorial service was held a week later, and she was buried at Fairhaven Memorial Park in Santa Ana, California, far from the family graves in Haarlem and Loenen.

Some who loved her pointed out that in Jewish tradition, to die on one’s birthday is sometimes regarded as a mark of a righteous life completed. It is the kind of pious gloss that gathers around the deaths of beloved people. Corrie herself would probably have smiled at it, and then pointed away from herself. She had long ago told her fellow prisoners that for those who belong to the Saviour, death is not a pit into which they fall but a tunnel into the light. She had watched her father go through that tunnel, and her sister. Now it was her turn.

For Reflection

Many of us fear the kind of ending Corrie had: years of helplessness and silence, dependent on others for everything. Her life does not make that ending less hard. But it suggests that such years need not be empty. They can be a continuation of the same faith, in a different key: a witness of patience instead of preaching, of receiving instead of giving.

“Even to old age I am he, and even to hoar hairs will I carry you.” The God who carried Corrie through Ravensbrück carried her through her last five silent years too. He does not stop carrying his people when they can no longer work for him.

fields.title: The Legacy of Corrie ten Boom
fields.body_html:
“And a man shall be as a hiding-place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest, as streams of water in a dry place, as the shade of a great rock in a weary land.”

— Isaiah 32:2, ASV

The House in the Barteljorisstraat

On 15 April 1988, what would have been Corrie’s ninety-sixth birthday, the Beje opened as a museum. It is run by a foundation, and in recent years the old watch shop at the front has been brought back into it. Visitors from all over the world climb the narrow stairs to the little bedroom at the top of the house and look through the low opening under the cupboard shelf into the hiding place. The house appears in the official canon of Dutch history, the list of places and events that every Dutch schoolchild is meant to know.

On the front of the house is a memorial plaque. It records members of the family who died because of the war. Betsie’s entry gives her dates and the one word Ravensbrück. Christiaan’s, the nephew called Kik, gives April 1945, with the place of death recorded as unknown. For many years the plaque and the museum were among the few public reminders in Haarlem of what had happened in that house.

In 2007 Yad Vashem recognised Casper and Betsie ten Boom as Righteous Among the Nations, forty years after it had honoured Corrie. The whole household, not only its most famous member, had risked everything for their Jewish neighbours.

What Corrie Would Have Wanted Remembered

It is not hard to guess what Corrie herself would have wanted her legacy to be, because she spent forty years saying it. She would not have wanted people to remember her courage, which she always played down. She would have wanted them to remember the faithfulness of God, who had been with her in the darkest place human beings have ever made. She would have wanted them to remember Betsie. And she would have wanted them to hear the message the two of them had learned there: that God’s love is deeper than any pit, that Jesus is victor, and that forgiveness is possible because God gives it.

This book has tried to honour that wish while also telling the truth about the sources. It has noted which stories come from her earliest account and which appear only in the later books. It has corrected popular claims that the records do not support. It has refused to make her a plaster saint. None of that diminishes her. The core of her story, the rescue, the raid, the prisons, the deaths, the release, and the forty years of witness, is confirmed at every point by independent records. The famous scenes that rest on her own later memory are consistent with everything else she wrote and did. And the real woman who emerges is more encouraging than any legend. She was often afraid, sometimes selfish by her own admission, and always dependent on God.

Ordinary People

Perhaps the most important thing about the ten Booms is how ordinary they were. They were not political activists or heroes of the resistance in the usual sense. They were an elderly watchmaker and his two unmarried daughters, pious and old-fashioned, who had spent their lives on small things. They wound clocks, ran girls’ clubs, taught disabled people, took in foster children, and prayed each week for Jerusalem. When the crisis came, they did what they had always done, but at the cost of everything.

That should encourage anyone who feels that their own life is too small to matter. The courage the ten Booms showed in 1943 and 1944 did not come from nowhere. It was built over decades of ordinary faithfulness. Most of us will never face what they faced. But all of us are building, day by day, the kind of people we will be if a test ever comes.

The Two Hiding Places

The title by which the world knows Corrie’s story has a double meaning, and it is worth ending with both.

The first hiding place was a space behind a false wall in a bedroom in Haarlem. It was built by an architect whose real name is still unknown, and it did exactly what it was meant to do. Six people stood in it for two and a half days while the house was searched and then guarded, and they were not found. It was a real work of courage and skill. But it could not save everyone. It could not save Mary van Itallie, re-arrested within days and murdered at Auschwitz, or the family who built it. Every human hiding place, in the end, is like that. It is precious and partial, and it cannot finally protect.

The second hiding place was the one Corrie found when the first one could no longer help her. She was alone in a cell at Scheveningen, standing in the freezing dark at roll-call in Ravensbrück, and watching her sister’s body carried out in a sheet. There she found that God himself was her hiding place. That did not mean she escaped suffering. She did not, and Betsie did not. It meant that in the middle of suffering there was a presence that could not be taken away. “Thou art my hiding-place and my shield: I hope in thy word” (Psalm 119:114, ASV).

The verse at the head of this chapter joins the two. Isaiah looks forward to a righteous king, and to the kind of people who live under his rule: “a man shall be as a hiding-place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest, as streams of water in a dry place, as the shade of a great rock in a weary land” (Isaiah 32:2, ASV). Christians have long heard in those words a picture of Christ himself, the true hiding place. But the prophet also describes what human beings become when they live under God’s rule. They become hiding places for others.

That is what the ten Booms were. For a few months in 1943 and 1944, a narrow house in Haarlem was a hiding place from the wind for people being hunted to death. And for forty years afterwards, a woman who had lost almost everything became a shelter for others. She was a hiding place for former prisoners, for displaced Germans, and for collaborators no one else would take in. She was a shelter for guards who asked her forgiveness, and for anyone anywhere who needed to hear that there is no darkness so deep that God is not deeper still. She could be that for others because she had found her own hiding place in God.

For Reflection

The Portraits of Courage series began with Watchman Nee, who endured twenty years in a Chinese prison. It continued with John Hyde, whose courage was spent on his knees in the Punjab. Corrie ten Boom’s courage was different again. It was the courage of an ordinary household that opened its door when opening it could cost everything, and the courage of a survivor who chose forgiveness over hatred.

We are not called to her life. But we are called to be, in our own places, what Isaiah described: a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, and streams of water in a dry place. And we can only be that for others if we have first found, as she did, that God himself is our hiding place.

fields.title: Appendix A: Lessons from the Life of Corrie ten Boom
fields.body_html:
“Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee; because he trusteth in thee.”

— Isaiah 26:3, ASV

The lessons below gather the themes of this book so that readers can return to them. They are not a method. Corrie ten Boom would have been the first to say that her life was not a pattern to copy, but a witness to the faithfulness of God. Each lesson rests on Scripture, not on her example alone.

1. Faithfulness Is Built in Small Things

The courage of 1943 was built by a century of small faithfulness: a weekly prayer for Jerusalem, a trade kept honestly, and a crowded table with room for one more. “He that is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10, ASV).

2. Pray for What God Loves

By family tradition, the ten Booms had prayed for the Jewish people for generations before anyone needed hiding. When the time came, they did not need to be persuaded that the Jews were their concern. “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: They shall prosper that love thee” (Psalm 122:6, ASV).

3. Disappointment Can Be Redirected

Corrie’s lost hope of marriage became, by her father’s counsel, love given another way to go, to many more people than one household could hold. “God setteth the solitary in families” (Psalm 68:6, ASV).

4. Serve the Least

Long before the war, Corrie gave her time to disabled people whom others overlooked. She defended their worth before a Gestapo officer. “Inasmuch as ye did it unto one of these my brethren, even these least, ye did it unto me” (Matthew 25:40, ASV).

5. You May Have Come for Such a Time as This

An old watchmaker and his daughters had no power, but they had a place, a house, and a network of trust. God did not need them, and yet he placed them there. “Who knoweth whether thou art not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14, ASV).

6. Open the Next Door

The rescue work began with one frightened person at the door, and then another. God rarely shows the whole road at once. “Deliver them that are carried away unto death” (Proverbs 24:11, ASV).

7. Fear God More Than Pharaoh

The midwives in Egypt refused to kill the children, and God dealt well with them. Christians may disagree about hard questions of truth-telling under tyranny. But no one is obliged to help carry out injustice. “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29, ASV).

8. Prepare Wisely, Live Joyfully

The Beje drilled with a stopwatch and also held concerts, classes, and cream-puff suppers. Practical preparation and joyful trust belong together. “Thou art my hiding-place; thou wilt preserve me from trouble; Thou wilt compass me about with songs of deliverance” (Psalm 32:7, ASV).

9. God Is Present in Solitude

In solitary confinement Corrie found a closeness to God she had never known. “When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up” (Psalm 27:10, ASV).

10. Every Soul Matters

Before a Gestapo officer who called her work with disabled people a waste of time, Corrie insisted that God’s love reaches the weak and despised. Her statement recorded that she would help anyone in need, of any race or creed, in obedience to Christ.

11. We See the Underside of the Embroidery

On the night of the executions at Vught, Corrie learned that we see only the tangled back of God’s work. One day we will see the pattern. “For now we see in a mirror, darkly; but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12, ASV).

12. Don’t Carry the Whole World’s Grief

At Vught Corrie learned that she was not asked to bear the sorrows of the whole world, only to bring them to God. “Casting all your anxiety upon him, because he careth for you” (1 Peter 5:7, ASV).

13. Give Thanks in Everything

Betsie gave thanks in Barracks 28. Whatever exactly she said about the fleas, her life was an exercise in thanksgiving. “In everything give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus to you-ward” (1 Thessalonians 5:18, ASV).

14. Give First, Even Out of Poverty

In a camp where survival seemed to require selfishness, Corrie gave her vitamins to thirty strangers a day. “The jar of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail” (1 Kings 17:16, ASV).

15. Beware the Ravensbrück That Destroys

Corrie saw selfishness as a subtler danger than cruelty. Need can teach us to pray, and it can also make us selfish. “not looking each of you to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:4, ASV).

16. God Is There Even in the Pit

Betsie died believing that no darkness is deeper than God’s love. “If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, thou art there” (Psalm 139:8, ASV).

17. Escape Is God’s Gift, However It Came

Whether Corrie’s release was a clerical error or an ordinary discharge, she knew she had been brought out of the snare. “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers” (Psalm 124:7, ASV).

18. Forgive Before You Feel It

Corrie wrote to the informer within months of Betsie’s death. Forgiveness is an act of the will, and the feelings follow. “Love your enemies, and pray for them that persecute you” (Matthew 5:44, ASV).

19. Overcome Evil with Good

She opened a home in Germany, preached to former guards, and took in those her neighbours rejected. “Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21, ASV).

20. The Love Is Given

In Munich she could not forgive, and asked God for his love, and it came. “The love of God hath been shed abroad in our hearts through the Holy Spirit which was given unto us” (Romans 5:5, ASV).

21. Tell What You Have Seen

For thirty years she told the same story in sixty countries, in season and out. “Preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2, ASV).

22. God Carries Us to the End

In her silent last years she was carried, as she had been at birth. “Even to old age I am he, and even to hoar hairs will I carry you” (Isaiah 46:4, ASV).

23. Become a Hiding Place for Others

Those who have found their hiding place in God can shelter others from the storm. “A man shall be as a hiding-place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest” (Isaiah 32:2, ASV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

— James 1:22, ASV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty weeks. Its purpose is not to make Corrie ten Boom an object of admiration, but to let her life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer.

Chapter 1 - The Beje

Central idea

A century of small faithfulness in a Haarlem watch shop, including a weekly prayer for Jerusalem begun in 1844, prepared the family for a test they could not foresee.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 122; Matthew 5:10; Luke 16:10.

Reflection

1. What do we pray for every week? 2. Whom do we make room for? 3. What small faithfulness are we building now?

Chapter 2 - A Father Among the Watches

Central idea

Casper ten Boom’s settled love for “God’s ancient people,” drawn from Scripture, was lived in ordinary courtesies long before it became dangerous.

Scriptures to revisit

Genesis 12:1-3; Romans 9:4-5; Romans 11:1-2, 29; 1 Peter 2:17; Philippians 1:21.

Reflection

1. Which of our convictions would we be willing to wear on our sleeve? 2. How do we speak of and treat the Jewish people?

Chapter 3 - The Youngest Daughter

Central idea

Loss of a mother and of a hoped-for marriage shaped Corrie deeply; her father taught her to let blocked love find another way.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 68:6; Isaiah 54:1; 2 Corinthians 1:3-4.

Reflection

1. Is there a blocked love or disappointment in your life? 2. Have you killed it, or asked God to redirect it?

Chapter 4 - The First Woman Watchmaker

Central idea

Twenty years of patient, precise work formed habits the underground would need, and made a shop into the perfect cover.

Scriptures to revisit

Luke 16:10; Colossians 3:23; Proverbs 22:29.

Reflection

1. How do you regard ordinary work? 2. Is it a waiting room, or a workshop where God forms you?

Chapter 5 - Clubs, Children, and the Least of These

Central idea

Girls’ clubs, classes for disabled people, and foster children were quiet works that turned out to be preparation.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 25:31-46; James 1:27.

Reflection

1. Who are the least in your community? 2. What habits of love are you forming in quiet years?

Chapter 6 - May 1940

Central idea

The occupation crept in step by step, and at each step it was easier to comply than to resist.

Scriptures to revisit

Esther 4:12-16; Proverbs 31:8-9.

Reflection

1. Where is it easier for you to comply than to speak? 2. Where might you have been placed for such a time as this?

Chapter 7 - The First Knock

Central idea

The rescue work began one frightened person at a time, until the Beje became a hub of the underground.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 24:11-12; Hebrews 13:1-3.

Reflection

1. Who is the next person God might send to your door? 2. What keeps you from opening it?

Chapter 8 - Ration Cards and Lies

Central idea

Hiding people required ration cards, false papers, and deception, and Christians, including the ten Booms, disagreed about lying.

Scriptures to revisit

Exodus 1:15-21; Joshua 2; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25; Acts 5:29; Romans 14:5.

Reflection

1. How do you hold together truthfulness and the protection of the vulnerable? 2. How do you disagree with fellow Christians without breaking fellowship?

Chapter 9 - The Angels’ Crib

Central idea

The hiding place was built and drilled with a stopwatch, while the household lived with music, classes, and laughter.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 32:6-7; Psalm 27:5.

Reflection

1. Where do you need both practical preparation and joyful trust? 2. What is your final hiding place?

Chapter 10 - 28 February 1944

Central idea

The raid: the hiding place held, but the house did not protect those who built it, and not all six survived.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 91.

Reflection

1. How do you read Psalm 91 in the light of suffering? 2. What does God promise, and what does he not?

Chapter 11 - “Father Was Released”

Central idea

Casper’s death, and Corrie’s solitary confinement, where she found God near in loneliness.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 27; Genesis 5:24; Proverbs 12:10.

Reflection

1. Where have you found God near in loneliness? 2. How did Corrie speak to the man who interrogated her?

Chapter 12 - Vught

Central idea

Reunion with Betsie, the society against grumbling, the executions, and the embroidery lesson.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 43:1-3; Philippians 2:14-15; John 21:18.

Reflection

1. What would it mean to see your present suffering as the underside of the embroidery? 2. What sorrows do you need to leave with God?

Chapter 13 - Barracks 28

Central idea

A hidden Bible, daily readings, the fleas story set beside the 1945 account, and thanksgiving in hell.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Thessalonians 5:16-18; Hebrews 13:5.

Reflection

1. What would it look like to give thanks in your present trial? 2. Do you look for God’s hand in everything?

Chapter 14 - The Bottle That Did Not Fail

Central idea

The vitamin bottle, told already in 1945, and the moral danger of selfishness in the camp.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Kings 17:8-16; Luke 4:25-26; Philippians 2:4.

Reflection

1. Where is the “Ravensbrück that destroys” at work in you? 2. What could you give out of your poverty?

Chapter 15 - Betsie

Central idea

Betsie’s serenity, her plans, her illness and death, and the saying “no pit so deep.”

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 139:7-12; Job 1:10, 21; 1 Corinthians 15.

Reflection

1. Who has been a hiding place for you? 2. How does your faith face death?

Chapter 16 - Entlassen

Central idea

The punishment roll-call, a week in the hospital barracks, release, the journey home, and the “clerical error” weighed.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 124.

Reflection

1. How do you give thanks for deliverances whose causes you do not understand?

Chapter 17 - A Letter to the Informer

Central idea

Liberation, pity for women whose heads were being shaved, and a letter of forgiveness written in June 1945.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 5:43-48; Romans 5:10; Romans 12:17-21; Ephesians 4:32.

Reflection

1. Is there someone you need to forgive before you feel like it? 2. Could you write the letter?

Chapter 18 - Homes for the Broken

Central idea

Bloemendaal, Darmstadt, and preaching to former guards: answering evil with good.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 12:14-21; Isaiah 61:4.

Reflection

1. Whom do you avoid because of wrongs done to you or yours? 2. What good could you do instead?

Chapter 19 - The Hand in Munich

Central idea

The famous handshake, told as her own later memory: forgiveness given by God when she could not give it.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 5:5-10; Matthew 18:21-35.

Reflection

1. Whom do you find impossible to forgive? 2. Will you tell God so, and ask for his love?

Chapter 20 - Sixty Countries

Central idea

Thirty years of travel, “Jesus is Victor,” The Hiding Place, honours, and the controversies.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Timothy 4:1-8; Colossians 2:15.

Reflection

1. What have you seen of God’s faithfulness? 2. Whom are you telling?

Chapter 21 - The Five Silent Years

Central idea

Strokes, silence, and being carried, echoing her mother’s last years.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 46:3-4; 2 Corinthians 4:16-18.

Reflection

1. How do you face the prospect of helplessness? 2. How can those years still be a witness?

Chapter 22 - The Legacy of Corrie ten Boom

Central idea

The museum, the Righteous Among the Nations, ordinary people, and the two hiding places.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 32:1-2; Psalm 119:114; Hebrews 11.

Reflection

1. Where have you found your hiding place? 2. For whom could you be a shelter from the storm?
